def: The process of putting software into use on a live system.
ex: The deployment is scheduled for Friday night.
nat: Automated deployments help us release code faster and with fewer errors.

mis.bad: We made the deploy yesterday.
mis.good: We did the deployment yesterday.
mis.why: 'Deploy' is mainly a verb; use 'deployment' as the noun.

def: A period when a system or service stops working.
ex: The outage lasted almost two hours and affected all customers.
nat: We need a better plan to prevent another outage during peak hours.

mis.bad: The system fell for two hours.
mis.good: The system was down for two hours.
mis.why: Use 'was down' or 'had an outage', not 'fell'.

def: The act of returning software to an earlier, working version.
ex: We did a rollback because the new release broke the login page.
nat: A quick rollback saved us from a long outage.

mis.bad: We need to make a roll-back of the version.
mis.good: We need to roll back the version.
mis.why: 'Roll back' (two words) is the verb; 'rollback' is the noun.

def: The time when a system is not available for use.
ex: We planned two hours of downtime for the database upgrade.
nat: Every minute of downtime costs the company money.

mis.bad: We had a downtime yesterday.
mis.good: We had some downtime yesterday.
mis.why: 'Downtime' is uncountable; don't use 'a downtime'.

def: A small update that fixes a problem in software.
ex: Install the security patch before the end of the day.
nat: The vendor released a patch within hours of the report.

mis.bad: Please make the patch in all servers.
mis.good: Please apply the patch to all servers.
mis.why: Use 'apply/install a patch' and 'to' the servers.

def: A weakness that attackers can use to break into a system.
ex: The scan found a critical vulnerability in the login service.
nat: Hackers exploited a known vulnerability that nobody had fixed.

mis.bad: Hackers explore the vulnerability of the system.
mis.good: Hackers exploit the vulnerability.
mis.why: Attackers 'exploit' a vulnerability; 'explore' is wrong.

def: A temporary way to avoid a problem without fixing its cause.
ex: There is no fix yet, but we found a workaround for the bug.
nat: As a workaround, users can export the report manually.

mis.bad: We found a work around for the bug.
mis.good: We found a workaround for the bug.
mis.why: As a noun, 'workaround' is one word; 'work around' (two words) is the verb.

def: The main reason why a problem happens.
ex: The root cause of the crash was a memory leak.
nat: We ran a review to find the root cause before making changes.

mis.bad: The root of the cause was the network.
mis.good: The root cause was the network.
mis.why: Say 'root cause', not 'root of the cause'.

def: An event that causes a problem or disrupts normal work.
ex: The security team is handling a serious incident.
nat: Please write an incident report after the outage ends.

mis.bad: The incident happened by a bug.
mis.good: The incident was caused by a bug.
mis.why: Use 'caused by' to give the reason; 'by' alone after 'happened' is wrong.

def: An extra copy of data that you keep in case the original is lost.
ex: Always keep a backup of your important files.
nat: The backup runs automatically every night at 2 a.m.

mis.bad: I will do a backup of the files.
mis.good: I will back up the files.
mis.why: As a verb, write 'back up' (two words); 'backup' is the noun.

def: To bring a system or data back to its earlier state.
ex: We restored the database from last night's backup.
nat: After the crash, it took us six hours to get everything restored.

mis.bad: I need to restaure the file.
mis.good: I need to restore the file.
mis.why: The word is 'restore', not 'restaure'.

def: A security system that blocks unwanted network traffic.
ex: The firewall blocks all connections from unknown addresses.
nat: Ask the network team to open a port in the firewall for our new app.

mis.bad: The firewall blocks all the ports of the server.
mis.good: The firewall blocks all ports on the server.
mis.why: Say 'ports on a server'; don't use 'of' for this relationship.

def: A group of computers that work together as one system.
ex: We run the application on a cluster of five servers.
nat: If one node in the cluster fails, the others take over its work.

mis.bad: We installed a cluster in five servers.
mis.good: We set up a cluster of five servers.
mis.why: Use 'cluster of' to say what it contains.

def: An automatic switch to a backup system when the main one fails.
ex: The failover worked and users never noticed the crash.
nat: We test the failover plan every quarter to make sure it works.

mis.bad: We did the fail over test.
mis.good: We ran a failover test.
mis.why: As a noun or modifier it is one word: 'failover'; 'fail over' is the verb.

def: The amount of data a network connection can carry at a time.
ex: The video call was poor because we had low bandwidth.
nat: I don't have the bandwidth to take on another project this week.

mis.bad: I have no bandwidth of time.
mis.good: I don't have the bandwidth.
mis.why: Informally, 'bandwidth' alone means available time or energy.

def: The delay before data starts to transfer after a request.
ex: High latency made the online game almost impossible to play.
nat: We moved the server closer to users to reduce latency.

mis.bad: The latency is very high of the connection.
mis.good: The connection has very high latency.
mis.why: Say 'has high latency'; don't add 'of the connection'.

def: An event where someone gets into private data without permission.
ex: The company announced a data breach affecting a million users.
nat: A single weak password can lead to a serious breach.

mis.bad: They did a breach in our system.
mis.good: They breached our system.
mis.why: Use 'breach' as a verb or 'suffer a breach', not 'do a breach'.

def: To change data into a code so that only allowed people can read it.
ex: All customer data is encrypted before it is stored.
nat: We encrypt backups to protect them if they are ever stolen.

mis.bad: The data is criptografed.
mis.good: The data is encrypted.
mis.why: The English verb is 'encrypt'.

def: Able to handle more users or work without problems.
ex: We need a scalable solution that works for ten or ten thousand users.
nat: The new architecture is cheap and highly scalable.

mis.bad: The system is escalable.
mis.good: The system is scalable.
mis.why: 'Escalable' is Portuguese; in English it is 'scalable'.

def: Extra equipment that keeps a system running if something fails.
ex: The data center has full power redundancy.
nat: Redundancy is expensive, but it protects us from single points of failure.

mis.bad: We have redundancy of servers.
mis.good: We have server redundancy.
mis.why: Use a noun modifier: 'server redundancy'.

def: To prove who you are before getting access to a system.
ex: Users must authenticate with a password and a code.
nat: The app failed to authenticate me, so I couldn't log in.

mis.bad: You need to autenticate first.
mis.good: You need to authenticate first.
mis.why: The spelling has 'th': authenticate.

def: A point in a process that slows everything down.
ex: The database is the main bottleneck in our system.
nat: Approvals have become a bottleneck for the whole team.

mis.bad: The process has a bottle neck.
mis.good: The process has a bottleneck.
mis.why: Write 'bottleneck' as one word.

def: To watch something regularly to check its condition.
ex: We monitor the servers 24 hours a day.
nat: The team monitors error rates after every release.

mis.bad: We acompany the servers all day.
mis.good: We monitor the servers all day.
mis.why: 'Acompanhar' here is 'monitor' or 'track', not 'accompany'.

def: To search for the cause of a problem in order to fix it.
ex: I spent an hour troubleshooting the printer.
nat: Start by troubleshooting the network before you blame the application.

mis.bad: I will troubleshoot the problem of the VPN.
mis.good: I will troubleshoot the VPN.
mis.why: 'Troubleshoot' takes the system directly.

def: To replace something with a newer or better version.
ex: We upgraded the servers to handle more traffic.
nat: The old laptops should be upgraded before the new software arrives.

mis.bad: We upgraded the system for the latest version.
mis.good: We upgraded the system to the latest version.
mis.why: Use 'to' before the new version.

def: To move data or systems from one place or platform to another.
ex: We migrated all our services to the cloud last year.
nat: The data was migrated overnight without any loss.

mis.bad: We migrated for the cloud.
mis.good: We migrated to the cloud.
mis.why: Use 'to' with the destination.

def: The username and password used to log in to a system.
ex: Never share your login credentials with anyone.
nat: The attackers stole credentials from several employees.

mis.bad: My credential is wrong.
mis.good: My credentials are wrong.
mis.why: In this meaning, 'credentials' is normally plural.

def: Software made to damage a computer or steal information.
ex: The malware spread through an infected email attachment.
nat: Our antivirus detected malware on two laptops this morning.

mis.bad: The computer has a malware.
mis.good: The computer has malware.
mis.why: 'Malware' is uncountable; no 'a'.

def: A scam that uses fake emails to steal personal information.
ex: Employees receive training on how to spot phishing emails.
nat: The phishing message looked like it came from our bank.

mis.bad: I fell in a phishing.
mis.good: I fell for a phishing scam.
mis.why: Use 'fall for' a scam, not 'fall in'.

def: Following laws, rules, or standards that apply to a business.
ex: Compliance with data protection laws is mandatory for us.
nat: The audit checks compliance with security policies every year.

mis.bad: We must be in compliance of the law.
mis.good: We must be in compliance with the law.
mis.why: Use 'compliance with', not 'of'.

def: A level or point at which something changes or starts.
ex: An alert is sent when CPU use passes the 90% threshold.
nat: Once the error rate crosses that threshold, the system starts sending alerts.

mis.bad: The threshold of errors is five.
mis.good: The error threshold is five.
mis.why: Use a noun modifier instead of 'of errors'.

def: The amount of work or data a system processes in a given time.
ex: The new storage doubled our write throughput.
nat: Network throughput drops at peak times because of heavy traffic.

mis.bad: The system has a low throughputs.
mis.good: The system has low throughput.
mis.why: 'Throughput' is uncountable; it has no plural and no 'a'.

def: A collection of data used for analysis or to train a model.
ex: We trained the model on a dataset of two million images.
nat: The dataset contains customer records from the last five years.

mis.bad: A data set of the clients.
mis.good: A dataset of clients.
mis.why: 'Dataset' is usually written as one word.

def: An unfair tendency that makes results favor one side or group.
ex: The model showed bias against certain groups of applicants.
nat: Bias in training data can lead to unfair decisions.

mis.bad: The AI has a bias to women.
mis.good: The AI has a bias against women.
mis.why: Say 'bias against' or 'bias toward'.

def: A confident answer from an AI that is false or invented.
ex: The chatbot produced a hallucination and invented a fake source.
nat: Always check facts, because hallucinations are common in language models.

mis.bad: The AI hallucinated a information.
mis.good: The AI hallucinated some information.
mis.why: 'Information' is uncountable; don't use 'a'.

def: The text you give an AI so that it can respond.
ex: A clear prompt gives you a much better answer from the model.
nat: I rewrote my prompt and added an example to get better results.

mis.bad: I made a prompt for the AI.
mis.good: I wrote a prompt for the AI.
mis.why: Use 'write a prompt'.

def: To make a process work by itself using technology.
ex: We automated the monthly reports to save time.
nat: If you repeat a task every day, try to automate it.

mis.bad: We automatize the process.
mis.good: We automate the process.
mis.why: The verb is 'automate', not 'automatize'.

def: To connect different systems so that they work together.
ex: We integrated the payment tool with our website.
nat: The CRM integrates easily with most email platforms.

mis.bad: We integrated the tool to our system.
mis.good: We integrated the tool with our system.
mis.why: Use 'integrate with' for connecting two systems.

def: To set up software or equipment so it works as needed.
ex: I configured the server to restart automatically.
nat: The VPN is not configured correctly on my laptop.

mis.bad: I configured wrong the router.
mis.good: I configured the router incorrectly.
mis.why: The adverb goes after the object: 'incorrectly'.

def: Still available but not recommended and likely to be removed.
ex: This function is deprecated and will be removed next year.
nat: Using a deprecated library can create security risks.

mis.bad: This method is depreciated.
mis.good: This method is deprecated.
mis.why: 'Deprecated' = not recommended any more; 'depreciated' means lost value (like a car).

def: Old and still in use, often hard to change or replace.
ex: Our legacy system is over twenty years old.
nat: Many banks still depend on legacy software.

mis.bad: The legacy of the code is bad.
mis.good: The legacy code is bad.
mis.why: As an adjective, 'legacy' goes before the noun.

def: Able to recover quickly after a problem.
ex: We built a resilient system that survives server failures.
nat: Resilient teams stay calm and adapt when plans change.

mis.bad: The system is resilient of failures.
mis.good: The system is resilient to failures.
mis.why: Use 'resilient to'.

def: To reduce how serious or harmful something is.
ex: We added extra servers to mitigate the risk of overload.
nat: The team acted fast to mitigate the damage from the breach.

mis.bad: We need to mitigate the risk to zero.
mis.good: We need to mitigate the risk.
mis.why: 'Mitigate' means reduce, not remove completely.

def: To pass a problem to someone with more authority.
ex: If you cannot solve it in an hour, escalate the ticket to level 2.
nat: I escalated the issue to my manager because the client was angry.

mis.bad: I scaled the problem to my boss.
mis.good: I escalated the problem to my boss.
mis.why: Use 'escalate', not 'scale', for problems.

def: An official check of systems, records, or processes.
ex: The security audit found several weak passwords.
nat: We pass an external audit every year to keep our certification.

mis.bad: We made an audit in the system.
mis.good: We did an audit of the system.
mis.why: Use 'audit of' and 'do/conduct an audit'.

def: The date or time by which something must be finished.
ex: The deadline for the report is Friday at noon.
nat: We missed the deadline because the client changed the requirements.

mis.bad: We lost the deadline.
mis.good: We missed the deadline.
mis.why: Use 'miss' a deadline, not 'lose'.

def: A person or group affected by or interested in a project.
ex: We meet the key stakeholders every Monday to share updates.
nat: All stakeholders must approve the plan before we start.

mis.bad: The shareholders of the project must approve it.
mis.good: The stakeholders of the project must approve it.
mis.why: Shareholders own shares in a company; stakeholders are anyone affected by or interested in a project.

def: To discuss something to reach an agreement.
ex: She negotiated a better price with the supplier.
nat: We are negotiating the contract terms this week.

mis.bad: We negotiated about the price.
mis.good: We negotiated the price.
mis.why: 'Negotiate' takes the object directly, with no 'about'.

def: The amount of money planned for a purpose.
ex: We have a limited budget for new equipment.
nat: The project went over budget by twenty percent.

mis.bad: We are inside the budget.
mis.good: We are within budget.
mis.why: Say 'within budget' or 'on budget'.

def: A statement about what is likely to happen in the future.
ex: The sales forecast for next quarter looks strong.
nat: According to the forecast, demand will double by December.

mis.bad: The forecast of sales is good.
mis.good: The sales forecast is good.
mis.why: A noun modifier sounds more natural.

def: Not done or paid by the expected time.
ex: The invoice is two weeks overdue.
nat: I have three overdue tasks on my list.

mis.bad: The payment is late of two days.
mis.good: The payment is two days overdue.
mis.why: Put the time before 'overdue'.

def: To complete and provide what was promised.
ex: The team delivered the project on time.
nat: We always deliver high-quality results for our clients.

mis.bad: We delivered the project in the deadline.
mis.good: We delivered the project by the deadline.
mis.why: Use 'by' with a deadline.

def: To mention a subject or concern so people can discuss it.
ex: I raised my concerns about the timeline in the meeting.
nat: Several people raised questions about the budget.

mis.bad: I rised a question in the meeting.
mis.good: I raised a question in the meeting.
mis.why: 'Raise' is regular: raise, raised, raised.

def: A way of dealing with a task or problem.
ex: We need a new approach to customer support.
nat: A step-by-step approach makes the project easier to manage.

mis.bad: The approach for the problem is simple.
mis.good: The approach to the problem is simple.
mis.why: Use 'approach to'.

def: A limit or rule that restricts what you can do.
ex: Time is our biggest constraint on this project.
nat: Budget constraints forced us to reduce the scope.

mis.bad: We have a constraint of time.
mis.good: We have a time constraint.
mis.why: Use a noun modifier: 'time constraint'.

def: Something that is more important and must be done first.
ex: Customer safety is our top priority.
nat: Let's set clear priorities before the sprint starts.

mis.bad: This is a priority of the company.
mis.good: This is a priority for the company.
mis.why: Use 'priority for'.

def: To decide what is most important and do it first.
ex: You need to prioritize tasks when everything is urgent.
nat: We prioritized the bug fixes over new features.

mis.bad: I prioritized to finish the report.
mis.good: I prioritized finishing the report.
mis.why: 'Prioritize' is followed by a noun or -ing form, not 'to'.

def: To give a task or responsibility to someone else.
ex: A good manager knows when to delegate.
nat: I delegated the data entry to a new intern.

mis.bad: I delegated for my assistant.
mis.good: I delegated the task to my assistant.
mis.why: Use 'delegate something to someone'.

def: The amount of work someone has to do.
ex: My workload has doubled since two colleagues left.
nat: A heavy workload can lead to burnout.

mis.bad: I have a lot of workloads.
mis.good: I have a heavy workload.
mis.why: 'Workload' is usually singular; use 'heavy' (not 'a lot of') with it.

def: An important point or achievement in a project.
ex: We reached a key milestone when the first version went live.
nat: Each milestone has its own date and owner.

mis.bad: We reached an important mile stone.
mis.good: We reached an important milestone.
mis.why: Write 'milestone' as one word.

def: Something that is needed or demanded.
ex: A university degree is not a requirement for this job.
nat: We are still gathering the requirements from the client.

mis.bad: The requirement is to have experience of three years.
mis.good: The requirement is three years of experience.
mis.why: Put the number before 'years of experience'.

def: A formal plan or suggestion for others to consider.
ex: We sent the client a detailed proposal on Monday.
nat: The board rejected the proposal because it was too expensive.

mis.bad: I will do a proposal for the client.
mis.good: I will write a proposal for the client.
mis.why: Use 'write/submit a proposal'.

def: The final result of a process or action.
ex: We are happy with the outcome of the negotiation.
nat: The outcome depends on how fast we react.

mis.bad: The final outcome result was positive.
mis.good: The outcome was positive.
mis.why: 'Outcome' already means result; don't repeat both.

def: To succeed in reaching a goal after effort.
ex: We achieved all our sales targets this quarter.
nat: You can achieve more if you plan your week carefully.

mis.bad: We achieved to finish.
mis.good: We managed to finish.
mis.why: 'Achieve' takes a noun; use 'manage to' before a verb.

def: To move an event to a later time.
ex: We postponed the launch until next month.
nat: The meeting was postponed because the client was sick.

mis.bad: We postponed the meeting to anticipate.
mis.good: We brought the meeting forward.
mis.why: 'Postpone' means later; 'bring forward' means earlier.

def: To promise to do something or give your time to it.
ex: I can't commit to a date until I talk to my team.
nat: The company committed to reducing costs by ten percent.

mis.bad: I am committed with this project.
mis.good: I am committed to this project.
mis.why: Use 'committed to', not 'with'.

def: Required to explain your actions and take responsibility.
ex: Managers are accountable for their team's results.
nat: We must hold everyone accountable for meeting the deadline.

mis.bad: He is accountable of the budget.
mis.good: He is accountable for the budget.
mis.why: Use 'accountable for'.

def: To work together with others to achieve a goal.
ex: Our designers and developers collaborate closely.
nat: We collaborated with a university on this research.

mis.bad: We collaborate to the partner team.
mis.good: We collaborate with the partner team.
mis.why: Use 'collaborate with'.

def: A standard used to compare performance with others.
ex: We use industry benchmarks to measure our response time.
nat: Their results set a new benchmark for the whole sector.

mis.bad: We compared us with the industry benchmark.
mis.good: We compared ourselves with the industry benchmark.
mis.why: Use the reflexive 'ourselves' when subject and object are the same.

def: The total money a company earns from its business.
ex: Annual revenue grew by fifteen percent.
nat: Most of our revenue comes from subscriptions.

mis.bad: The revenues of the company is high.
mis.good: The company's revenue is high.
mis.why: 'Revenue' is usually singular and uncountable.

def: A document asking a customer to pay for goods or services.
ex: Please send the invoice by the end of the month.
nat: We still haven't received payment for the last invoice.

mis.bad: I will make the invoice to the client.
mis.good: I will send the invoice to the client.
mis.why: Use 'send/issue an invoice'.

def: A legal agreement between two or more parties.
ex: Both companies signed the contract on Tuesday.
nat: The contract ends in December, so we should discuss a renewal.

mis.bad: We closed the contract yesterday.
mis.good: We signed the contract yesterday.
mis.why: Use 'sign a contract'.

def: To make a process simpler and faster.
ex: We streamlined the approval process to save time.
nat: The new tool streamlines reporting for the whole department.

mis.bad: We need to streamline up the process.
mis.good: We need to streamline the process.
mis.why: 'Streamline' takes no particle.

def: To pay another company to do work for your business.
ex: The company outsourced its customer support to a call center.
nat: Many firms outsource IT services to reduce costs.

mis.bad: We tercerize the support.
mis.good: We outsource the support.
mis.why: The English verb for 'terceirizar' is 'outsource'.

def: To make something easier to understand.
ex: Could you clarify what you mean by 'urgent'?
nat: I'll send an email to clarify the next steps.

mis.bad: Can you clarify me this?
mis.good: Can you clarify this for me?
mis.why: 'Clarify' doesn't take a person as direct object.

def: To help a new employee or customer get started.
ex: We onboarded five new engineers last month.
nat: It takes two weeks to onboard a new customer.

mis.bad: We did the onboard of the new employee.
mis.good: We onboarded the new employee.
mis.why: 'Onboard' is the verb; the noun is 'onboarding' (We did the onboarding).

def: The time needed to finish a task and return it.
ex: The turnaround for design requests is two days.
nat: We offer a fast turnaround on all support tickets.

mis.bad: The turn around for requests is two days.
mis.good: The turnaround for requests is two days.
mis.why: As a noun, 'turnaround' is one word.

def: An amount that is less than what you need or expected.
ex: There is a shortfall of two hundred thousand dollars in the budget.
nat: The shortfall in sales forced us to cut costs.

mis.bad: There is a short fall in sales.
mis.good: There is a shortfall in sales.
mis.why: Write 'shortfall' as one word.

def: To use something you have in order to get a benefit.
ex: We can leverage our existing data to improve the product.
nat: The team leveraged cloud tools to launch in just a month.

mis.bad: We can leverage of our existing data.
mis.good: We can leverage our existing data.
mis.why: 'Leverage' is a transitive verb here; no 'of'.

def: To make sure that plans or ideas agree with each other.
ex: We need to align our goals with the company strategy.
nat: Let's meet to align on priorities before the launch.

mis.bad: We need to align about the priorities.
mis.good: We need to align on the priorities.
mis.why: Use 'align on' a topic or 'align with' a person or plan.

def: The range of work or topics that a project covers.
ex: The scope of the project grew without extra budget.
nat: Adding new features is outside the scope of this contract.

mis.bad: This is out of the scope.
mis.good: This is out of scope.
mis.why: Say 'out of scope' (no 'the') or 'outside the scope'.

def: Feeling that there is too much to deal with.
ex: I feel overwhelmed by the number of emails I get.
nat: She was overwhelmed with work after the merger.

mis.bad: I am overwhelmed of work.
mis.good: I am overwhelmed with work.
mis.why: Use 'overwhelmed by' or 'with'.

def: Able to be trusted to work well or do what is promised.
ex: We need a reliable internet connection for the call.
nat: He is a reliable colleague who always meets deadlines.

mis.bad: The system is confiable.
mis.good: The system is reliable.
mis.why: 'Confiable' is not English; use 'reliable'.

def: Working well without wasting time, money, or effort.
ex: The new process is much more efficient than the old one.
nat: An efficient team can finish the task in half the time.

mis.bad: We need a more efficient way of work.
mis.good: We need a more efficient way to work.
mis.why: Use 'way to + verb' to say how to do something.

def: Leaving very little time, money, or space.
ex: We are working to a tight schedule this month.
nat: The budget is tight, so we can't hire anyone new.

mis.bad: We have a short deadline.
mis.good: We have a tight deadline.
mis.why: 'Short deadline' is understood, but 'tight deadline' is the natural collocation.

def: A belief about how something will or should happen.
ex: The product did not meet our expectations.
nat: It's important to set clear expectations with the client.

mis.bad: I have expectative of a raise.
mis.good: I have expectations of a raise.
mis.why: 'Expectativa' is 'expectation' in English.

def: A problem that delays or stops progress.
ex: The server failure was a major setback for the project.
nat: Despite the setback, we launched on schedule.

mis.bad: We had a set back in the project.
mis.good: We had a setback in the project.
mis.why: As a noun, 'setback' is one word.

def: Still happening or continuing now.
ex: We have an ongoing investigation into the issue.
nat: There are ongoing talks between the two companies.

mis.bad: The project is in going.
mis.good: The project is ongoing.
mis.why: Write 'ongoing' as one word.

def: Done carefully and completely, with attention to detail.
ex: The team did a thorough review of the code.
nat: She gave a thorough explanation of the new process.

mis.bad: We did a through analysis.
mis.good: We did a thorough analysis.
mis.why: 'Thorough' (careful) is different from 'through'.

def: Not willing to do something and slow to agree.
ex: The client was reluctant to sign without a trial period.
nat: Many managers are reluctant to try new tools.

mis.bad: I am reluctant in doing it.
mis.good: I am reluctant to do it.
mis.why: Use 'reluctant to' + verb.

def: A detailed plan of a trip, including places and times.
ex: Our itinerary includes two days in Lisbon and three in Porto.
nat: I sent my parents a copy of the itinerary so they knew where we'd be.

mis.bad: We made a roadmap for the trip.
mis.good: We made an itinerary for the trip.
mis.why: 'Roadmap' is a plan for a project; a detailed travel plan is an itinerary.

def: The bags and suitcases you take when you travel.
ex: The airline lost my luggage, so I had to buy new clothes.
nat: You can only take one piece of hand luggage on this flight.

mis.bad: I have two luggages.
mis.good: I have two pieces of luggage.
mis.why: Luggage is uncountable, so it has no plural.

def: The activity of visiting interesting places as a tourist.
ex: We spent the whole morning sightseeing in the old town.
nat: After a long flight, I wasn't in the mood for sightseeing.

mis.bad: We went to sightseeing yesterday.
mis.good: We went sightseeing yesterday.
mis.why: Say 'go sightseeing' without 'to'.

def: A place where you can stay, such as a hotel or an apartment.
ex: Accommodation in the city centre is very expensive in summer.
nat: We booked our accommodation three months before the trip.

mis.bad: We need to find an accommodation.
mis.good: We need to find accommodation.
mis.why: Accommodation is usually uncountable in British English and not used with 'an'.

def: A time when something happens later than expected.
ex: There was a two-hour delay because of heavy fog.
nat: Passengers should expect delays this weekend.

mis.bad: My flight had a retard of two hours.
mis.good: My flight had a delay of two hours.
mis.why: 'Retard' is a false friend of 'retardo' (and is offensive); use 'delay'.

def: To get on a plane, train, ship or bus.
ex: Passengers may now board the plane through gate 12.
nat: We boarded the ferry just before it left the port.

mis.bad: We embarked the plane at nine.
mis.good: We boarded the plane at nine.
mis.why: 'Embark' needs 'on' ('embark on a ship') and sounds formal; 'board' takes the vehicle directly.

def: Money that is given back to you when you return something or cancel a service.
ex: The hotel gave us a full refund after the room turned out to be dirty.
nat: I'm still waiting for my refund from the airline.

mis.bad: I want a reimbursement of my ticket.
mis.good: I want a refund for my ticket.
mis.why: A refund is money returned for something you bought or cancelled; reimbursement is repayment of money you spent for someone (e.g. work expenses).

def: A small thing you buy to remember a place you visited.
ex: I bought a small magnet as a souvenir of our trip to Rome.
nat: The market was full of cheap souvenirs.

mis.bad: I bought a souvenir to my mother.
mis.good: I bought a souvenir for my mother.
mis.why: Use 'for' the person who receives the gift.

def: The place where someone or something is going.
ex: Thailand is a popular holiday destination for young travellers.
nat: We finally reached our destination after twelve hours on the road.

mis.bad: My destiny is Paris this summer.
mis.good: My destination is Paris this summer.
mis.why: 'Destiny' means fate; 'destination' is where you are going.

def: A short stop between two flights during a journey.
ex: We had a six-hour layover in Dubai on the way to India.
nat: During the layover, I walked around the airport to stretch my legs.

mis.bad: We made a scale in Miami.
mis.good: We had a layover in Miami.
mis.why: 'Scale' is a false friend of 'escala'; use layover or stopover.

def: The money you pay to travel on a bus, train, plane or taxi.
ex: The train fare to the airport is only five dollars.
nat: Bus fares went up again at the start of the year.
fam: fare (verb, to do well or badly)

mis.bad: The fare of the bus is two dollars.
mis.good: The bus fare is two dollars.
mis.why: Use a noun modifier: 'bus fare'.

def: Full of people.
ex: The metro was so crowded that I couldn't find a seat.
nat: We left the beach early because it was getting too crowded.

mis.bad: The bus was too much crowded.
mis.good: The bus was too crowded.
mis.why: Use 'too' alone before an adjective, not 'too much'.

def: To walk slowly around a place without a clear plan.
ex: We wandered through the narrow streets without a map.
nat: I love to wander around a new city on my first day.

mis.bad: We wandered by the streets all afternoon.
mis.good: We wandered through the streets all afternoon.
mis.why: Use 'through' or 'around' with wander.

def: The natural things you see in a place, like mountains, trees and rivers.
ex: The scenery along the coast was absolutely breathtaking.
nat: We took the slow train just to enjoy the scenery.

mis.bad: The sceneries were beautiful.
mis.good: The scenery was beautiful.
mis.why: Scenery is uncountable and has no plural.

def: An arrangement to keep a table, room or seat for you.
ex: I made a reservation for four people at eight o'clock.
nat: Do you have a reservation, or would you like to wait for a table?

mis.bad: I did a reservation at the restaurant.
mis.good: I made a reservation at the restaurant.
mis.why: The collocation is 'make a reservation', not 'do'.

def: A small job that you must do regularly, especially at home.
ex: Washing the dishes is my least favourite chore.
nat: We share the household chores equally.

mis.bad: I need to do the home tasks today.
mis.good: I need to do the chores today.
mis.why: 'Home tasks' is not used for housework; say 'chores' or 'housework'.

def: To take something from someone and give it back later.
ex: Can I borrow your charger? My phone is about to die.
nat: She borrowed a book from the library last week.

mis.bad: Can you borrow me your pen?
mis.good: Can you lend me your pen? / Can I borrow your pen?
mis.why: You borrow FROM someone, but you lend TO someone.

def: To give something to someone for a short time.
ex: Could you lend me twenty dollars until Friday?
nat: He lent his car to his brother for the weekend.

mis.bad: He lended me his bike.
mis.good: He lent me his bike.
mis.why: The past form of lend is irregular: lend, lent, lent.

def: The regular trip between your home and your work or school.
ex: My commute takes about an hour each way.
nat: I read on the train to make the most of my commute.

mis.bad: My commute to the work takes one hour.
mis.good: My commute to work takes one hour.
mis.why: Say 'to work' without 'the'.

def: To deal with a difficult situation successfully.
ex: She finds it hard to cope with the pressure of her new job.
nat: How do you cope with so much stress?

mis.bad: I can't cope it.
mis.good: I can't cope with it.
mis.why: Cope is always followed by 'with'.

def: The way your parents raised you and taught you how to behave.
ex: He had a strict upbringing, with very clear rules at home.
nat: My upbringing made me value honesty above everything.

mis.bad: He has a good creation from his parents.
mis.good: He had a good upbringing.
mis.why: 'Creation' is a false friend of 'criação'; use upbringing.

def: A person you know a little, but who is not a close friend.
ex: He's just an acquaintance from work, not a close friend.
nat: I met a few new acquaintances at the party.

mis.bad: He is my known from college.
mis.good: He is an acquaintance from college.
mis.why: Use 'acquaintance' for a person you know slightly, not 'known'.

def: To speak angrily with someone because you disagree.
ex: My brother and I argue about who should wash the car.
nat: They argued for an hour about where to spend the holidays.

mis.bad: I discussed with my sister yesterday.
mis.good: I argued with my sister yesterday.
mis.why: 'Discuss' means to talk about something calmly; 'argue' means to disagree angrily.

def: To tell someone that you are sorry for something you did.
ex: He apologized for being late and promised it wouldn't happen again.
nat: You should apologize to her before it gets worse.

mis.bad: I apologize you for the delay.
mis.good: I apologize to you for the delay.
mis.why: You apologize TO a person FOR something.

def: Unhappy because someone has something that you want, or because you fear losing someone's love.
ex: She felt jealous when her friend got the job she wanted.
nat: He gets jealous every time she talks to other guys.

mis.bad: I am jealous with his success.
mis.good: I am jealous of his success.
mis.why: Jealous is followed by 'of', not 'with'.

def: To believe that someone is honest and will not hurt you.
ex: I trust my sister completely; she has never lied to me.
nat: It takes years to build trust and only a moment to destroy it.

mis.bad: I trust on him.
mis.good: I trust him.
mis.why: Trust as a verb takes a direct object, with no preposition.

def: Feeling thankful for something someone did for you.
ex: I'm so grateful for your help with the move.
nat: She was grateful that her neighbours looked after the dog.

mis.bad: I'm grateful by your help.
mis.good: I'm grateful for your help.
mis.why: Use 'grateful for' something and 'grateful to' someone.

def: Uncomfortable or embarrassing, making you feel nervous.
ex: There was an awkward silence after he asked about her ex.
nat: I felt awkward at the party because I didn't know anyone.

mis.bad: I felt awkwardly at the party.
mis.good: I felt awkward at the party.
mis.why: After 'feel', use the adjective 'awkward', not the adverb.

def: Refusing to change your mind or your behaviour even when others ask you to.
ex: My father is so stubborn that he never admits he is wrong.
nat: Don't be so stubborn; just ask for directions.

mis.bad: My dad is a stubborn.
mis.good: My dad is stubborn.
mis.why: 'Stubborn' is an adjective, not a noun.

def: Casual talk about other people's private lives, often not kind or not true.
ex: I don't like office gossip, so I stay away from it.
nat: There's a lot of gossip about the neighbours at the moment.

mis.bad: She told me a lot of fofocas about him.
mis.good: She told me a lot of gossip about him.
mis.why: Gossip is uncountable; do not use a plural form.

def: A meeting of people who have not seen each other for a long time.
ex: We're planning a school reunion for next summer.
nat: The family reunion was full of laughter and old stories.

mis.bad: I had a reunion with my boss at ten.
mis.good: I had a meeting with my boss at ten.
mis.why: A reunion is when people meet again after a long time, not a work meeting.

def: A line of people waiting for something, one behind the other.
ex: There was a long queue outside the museum.
nat: We joined the queue for tickets and waited almost an hour.

mis.bad: We stayed in the queue for tickets.
mis.good: We stood in the queue for tickets.
mis.why: Use 'stand in a queue' or 'wait in a queue'; 'queue' is the British word, and American English says 'line'.

def: To come together in one place, or to bring things or people together.
ex: The whole family gathers at my grandmother's house every Sunday.
nat: A crowd gathered outside the building to see the celebrity.

mis.bad: We gathered us in the kitchen.
mis.good: We gathered in the kitchen.
mis.why: 'Gather' (to come together) is intransitive; no reflexive pronoun.

def: All the people who live together in one home.
ex: There are five people in my household, including two teenagers.
nat: Every household in the area received a letter from the council.

mis.bad: The government helps low-income houses.
mis.good: The government helps low-income households.
mis.why: 'House' is the building; 'household' means the people living together.

pt: guardar ressentimento de; ficar magoado com
def: To feel angry or bitter about something you think is unfair.
ex: She resented her brother for getting all the attention.
nat: I resent having to work every weekend for no extra pay.

mis.bad: She resented to her brother.
mis.good: She resented her brother.
mis.why: 'Resent' is transitive; no 'to'. It is a false friend of 'ressentir'.

def: A sign in your body that shows you have an illness.
ex: A sore throat and fever are common symptoms of the flu.
nat: If your symptoms get worse, you should see a doctor.

mis.bad: I have some sintoms of cold.
mis.good: I have some symptoms of a cold.
mis.why: Spelling: symptom has a 'y' and ends in '-om'.

def: To become healthy again after being ill or injured.
ex: It took him six weeks to recover from the operation.
nat: She is recovering well and should be home soon.

mis.bad: He recovered his health of the flu.
mis.good: He recovered from the flu.
mis.why: Use 'recover from' an illness.

def: A medical condition that makes you sick when you eat or touch something.
ex: I have a nut allergy, so I always check the ingredients.
nat: Pollen allergies get worse in spring.

mis.bad: I have allergy of peanuts.
mis.good: I have an allergy to peanuts.
mis.why: Use 'allergy to' something.

def: A paper from a doctor that lets you buy a certain medicine.
ex: You need a prescription to buy these strong painkillers.
nat: I picked up my prescription at the pharmacy on my way home.

mis.bad: The doctor gave me a recipe for the antibiotics.
mis.good: The doctor gave me a prescription for the antibiotics.
mis.why: 'Recipe' is only for cooking; a medical 'receita' is a prescription.

def: A state of extreme tiredness caused by working too hard for a long time.
ex: After years of overtime, she ended up with burnout and took a month off.
nat: Taking regular breaks can help you avoid burnout.

mis.bad: He is burnout.
mis.good: He is burned out.
mis.why: 'Burnout' is the noun; the adjective is 'burned out' (or 'burnt out').

def: A problem that makes it difficult to fall asleep or stay asleep.
ex: He has suffered from insomnia ever since he lost his job.
nat: Drinking coffee late at night can cause insomnia.

mis.bad: I have an insomnia.
mis.good: I have insomnia.
mis.why: 'Insomnia' is uncountable; no 'an'.

def: A treatment that makes an illness go away completely.
ex: Scientists are still searching for a cure for the common cold.
nat: There is no cure for this disease, but the treatment helps.

mis.bad: Rest is the best cure to a cold.
mis.good: Rest is the best cure for a cold.
mis.why: Use 'cure for' an illness.

def: A session of physical exercise.
ex: My workout at the gym lasted about an hour.
nat: I like to do a quick workout before breakfast.

mis.bad: I'm doing a training in the gym.
mis.good: I'm doing a workout at the gym.
mis.why: For exercise sessions use 'workout'; 'training' sounds like a course or professional practice.

def: Containing substances that are good for your health and growth.
ex: School lunches should be cheap, tasty and nutritious.
nat: Beans are a cheap and nutritious source of protein.

mis.bad: Fruit is very nutritive.
mis.good: Fruit is very nutritious.
mis.why: 'Nutritive' is rare and technical; use 'nutritious' for food.

def: To have enough money to buy or do something.
ex: We can't afford a new car right now.
nat: She couldn't afford to pay the rent this month.

mis.bad: I can't afford buy it.
mis.good: I can't afford to buy it.
mis.why: Afford is followed by 'to + verb' or a noun.

def: The price a person or company says they will charge for a job.
ex: The plumber gave us a quote of two hundred dollars for the repair.
nat: Can you send me a quote before you start the work?

mis.bad: I asked the plumber for a budget.
mis.good: I asked the plumber for a quote.
mis.why: In Portuguese 'orçamento' covers both; in English a price for a job is a 'quote' or 'estimate', while 'budget' is your own spending plan.

def: Money that you owe to a person or a bank.
ex: He is still paying off the debt from his student loan.
nat: Many young people start their careers in debt.

mis.bad: He is in debts with the bank.
mis.good: He is in debt to the bank.
mis.why: 'In debt' is uncountable; use 'debt', not 'debts', with 'in'.

def: The money a person earns, usually in a month or a year.
ex: His monthly income barely covers the rent.
nat: Families on a low income can get help from the government.

mis.bad: My incomes are low.
mis.good: My income is low.
mis.why: Income is usually singular when talking about one person's earnings.

def: Money that you spend on something.
ex: Rent is our biggest monthly expense.
nat: Travelling alone can be a big expense.

mis.bad: My expenses is too high for a family.
mis.good: My expenses are too high for a family.
mis.why: 'Expenses' is plural; use 'are'.

def: A loan from a bank that you use to buy a house.
ex: They took out a thirty-year mortgage to buy their first home.
nat: Our monthly mortgage payment is almost half of my salary.

mis.bad: I did a financing to buy my house.
mis.good: I took out a mortgage to buy my house.
mis.why: 'Financing' is not used like this; for a home loan say 'mortgage'.

def: Money that you have saved, usually in a bank.
ex: She used her savings to start a small bakery.
nat: He spent all his savings on a new motorbike.

mis.bad: I have a lot of saving in the bank.
mis.good: I have a lot of savings in the bank.
mis.why: Use the plural 'savings' for the money you have saved.

def: Something that you buy for much less than its normal price.
ex: At that price, the jacket was a real bargain.
nat: I found some great bargains at the end-of-season sale.

mis.bad: I did a good bargain on this jacket.
mis.good: I got a real bargain on this jacket.
mis.why: You 'get' or 'find' a bargain; 'do a bargain' is not natural.

def: To have to pay money back to someone.
ex: I owe my sister fifty dollars from last month.
nat: How much do we still owe the bank?

mis.bad: I owe to him some money.
mis.good: I owe him some money.
mis.why: Owe takes the person directly, with no 'to' before them.

def: An amount of money that you pay for a service or to join something.
ex: The bank charges a small fee for each international transfer.
nat: There is no entrance fee on the first Sunday of the month.

mis.bad: They charge a tax to use the card.
mis.good: They charge a fee to use the card.
mis.why: A 'tax' goes to the government; a service charge is a 'fee'.

def: An important discovery or achievement that solves a problem.
ex: Researchers announced a major breakthrough in cancer treatment.
nat: After months of testing, the team finally had a breakthrough.

mis.bad: A breakthrough of cancer treatment was announced.
mis.good: A breakthrough in cancer treatment was announced.
mis.why: Use 'breakthrough in' a field.

def: Facts or signs that show something is true.
ex: There is strong evidence that exercise improves memory.
nat: The police didn't have enough evidence to arrest him.

mis.bad: We found many evidences of the problem.
mis.good: We found a lot of evidence of the problem.
mis.why: Evidence is uncountable; use 'a piece of evidence'.

def: A medicine that protects you from a disease.
ex: A new vaccine for the virus will be available next month.
nat: Children receive this vaccine when they are two months old.

mis.bad: I took the flu vaccine yesterday.
mis.good: I got the flu vaccine yesterday.
mis.why: Say 'get a vaccine' or 'get vaccinated'; 'take a vaccine' is not natural.

def: Able to be replaced naturally, so it does not run out.
ex: Wind and solar are renewable sources of energy.
nat: The country plans to use only renewable energy by 2040.

mis.bad: The country needs more renewables energy.
mis.good: The country needs more renewable energy.
mis.why: Adjectives don't take -s and go before the noun.

def: The right to keep your personal life and information secret.
ex: Many people worry about their privacy when they use social media.
nat: The new law gives users more control over their privacy.

mis.bad: I need some privacities.
mis.good: I need some privacy.
mis.why: Privacy is uncountable.

def: A sudden start of something bad, like a disease or a war.
ex: Health officials are trying to control an outbreak of measles.
nat: The outbreak began in a small village and quickly spread.

mis.bad: There was an outbreak in measles.
mis.good: There was an outbreak of measles.
mis.why: Use 'outbreak of' a disease.

def: A small machine made for a particular purpose, like a phone or tablet.
ex: Please turn off all electronic devices before takeoff.
nat: This device can track how well you sleep.

mis.bad: I bought a new device of music.
mis.good: I bought a new music device.
mis.why: Use the noun before 'device' as a modifier, not 'of'.

def: To find or learn something for the first time.
ex: Scientists discovered a new species of frog in the rainforest.
nat: I discovered that I actually enjoy running in the morning.

mis.bad: I descovered the answer.
mis.good: I discovered the answer.
mis.why: Spelling: discover starts with 'dis-', not 'des-'.

def: A period of unusually hot weather that lasts several days.
ex: The city opened cooling centres during the heatwave.
nat: Another heatwave is expected next week, so drink plenty of water.

mis.bad: We had a heat wave of cold.
mis.good: We had a cold snap.
mis.why: A heatwave is always hot weather; use 'cold snap' for a short period of very cold weather.

def: A situation when there is not enough of something.
ex: Many hospitals are facing a shortage of nurses.
nat: A water shortage forced the town to limit showers.

mis.bad: There is a shortage in water.
mis.good: There is a shortage of water.
mis.why: Use 'shortage of' what is missing.

def: The series of events that make up the story of a book or film.
ex: The plot of the movie is hard to follow in the second half.
nat: I liked the acting, but the plot felt a bit predictable.

mis.bad: The history of the film is confusing.
mis.good: The plot of the film is confusing.
mis.why: 'History' refers to the past; use 'plot' or 'story' for a film's events.

def: All the actors in a film, play or TV show.
ex: The film has a great cast, including two Oscar winners.
nat: The whole cast came on stage to take a bow.

mis.bad: The film has a great actors team.
mis.good: The film has a great cast.
mis.why: 'Cast' is the group of actors in a production.

def: To make a film, song or product available to the public.
ex: The studio will release the film in theatres next March.
nat: The band released their new album last Friday.

mis.bad: The film will be launched in cinemas next week.
mis.good: The film will be released in cinemas next week.
mis.why: Films and albums are 'released'; 'launched' is for products, apps or campaigns.

def: A written opinion about a film, book, product or restaurant.
ex: The film got great reviews from critics.
nat: I always read the reviews before booking a hotel.

mis.bad: I read a critic of the film.
mis.good: I read a review of the film.
mis.why: 'Critic' is a person who reviews; 'critique' or 'review' is the text.

def: The people who watch or listen to a show, film or talk.
ex: The audience clapped for almost five minutes after the show.
nat: The programme is aimed at a younger audience.

mis.bad: I had an audience with the manager yesterday.
mis.good: I had a meeting with the manager yesterday.
mis.why: 'Audience' means the people watching, not a meeting.

def: A film or book that continues the story of an earlier one.
ex: The sequel was not as good as the original film.
nat: They are working on a sequel to last year's hit.

mis.bad: The film has a continuation.
mis.good: The film has a sequel.
mis.why: 'Continuation' is not used for a following film; say 'sequel'.

def: A film or TV programme that gives facts about real events or people.
ex: We watched a documentary about life in the Amazon.
nat: The documentary changed the way I think about food.

mis.bad: We watched a documentary of the Amazon.
mis.good: We watched a documentary about the Amazon.
mis.why: Use 'documentary about' a topic.

def: The music that is used in a film or video game.
ex: The soundtrack of the movie is just as famous as the film.
nat: I listen to the game's soundtrack when I study.

mis.bad: The sound band of the film was beautiful.
mis.good: The soundtrack of the film was beautiful.
mis.why: Use 'soundtrack', not 'sound band', for a film's music.

def: A public show of art or other objects.
ex: The museum has a new exhibition of modern photography.
nat: We queued for an hour to get into the exhibition.

mis.bad: We went to an exposition of paintings.
mis.good: We went to an exhibition of paintings.
mis.why: 'Exposition' is a false friend of 'exposição'; use exhibition.

def: To send out a programme on television or radio.
ex: The match will be broadcast live on national TV.
nat: The speech was broadcast to millions of viewers around the world.

mis.bad: The game was broadcasted yesterday.
mis.good: The game was broadcast yesterday.
mis.why: Broadcast has the same form in past and participle: broadcast, broadcast.

def: Large or important enough to have a clear effect.
ex: There has been a significant increase in house prices this year.
nat: Sleep has a significant effect on how well we learn.

mis.bad: The results were very significative.
mis.good: The results were very significant.
mis.why: The adjective is 'significant', not 'significative'.

def: Arriving or doing things at the correct time, not late.
ex: She is always punctual, so we can start the meeting on time.
nat: The trains here are very punctual, so don't be late.

mis.bad: He is very pontual for meetings.
mis.good: He is very punctual for meetings.
mis.why: The spelling is 'punctual' (with 'c'), not 'pontual'.

def: To usually do or be something.
ex: People tend to eat more when they are stressed.
nat: I tend to get nervous before big presentations.

mis.bad: I tend to going to bed late.
mis.good: I tend to go to bed late.
mis.why: 'Tend to' is followed by the base form of a verb.

def: A disadvantage or problem that makes something less attractive.
ex: The main drawback of living downtown is the noise.
nat: One drawback of the plan is that it will cost a lot.

mis.bad: That is a big draw back.
mis.good: That is a big drawback.
mis.why: As a noun, 'drawback' is one word.

def: A general change or direction in what people do or like.
ex: There is a growing trend towards working from home.
nat: Fashion trends change every season.

mis.bad: There is a tendency of increase in prices.
mis.good: There is a trend towards higher prices.
mis.why: For a general market or social direction use 'trend'; 'tendency' is more personal.

def: A worry about something important.
ex: Parents have expressed concern about the safety of the playground.
nat: Her main concern was that the children would be late.

mis.bad: I have a big preoccupation about the exam.
mis.good: I have a big concern about the exam.
mis.why: 'Preoccupation' is a false friend of 'preocupação'; use concern or worry.

def: A good or helpful result or effect.
ex: One benefit of cycling to work is that you save money.
nat: The new law will be of great benefit to families.

mis.bad: This will benefit to everyone.
mis.good: This will benefit everyone.
mis.why: As a verb, 'benefit' takes a direct object without 'to'.

def: To think something is true without checking.
ex: I assumed you knew about the party, so I didn't tell you.
nat: Don't assume that everyone shares your opinion.

mis.bad: I assumed my mistake.
mis.good: I admitted my mistake.
mis.why: 'Assume' in English means 'suppose'; to accept blame say 'admit' or 'take responsibility'.

def: To trust or depend on someone or something.
ex: You can always rely on her to tell the truth.
nat: Many small towns rely on tourism for their income.

mis.bad: I rely in my friends.
mis.good: I rely on my friends.
mis.why: Use the preposition 'on' with rely.

def: A result of something that happened, often a bad or serious one.
ex: Missing the deadline had serious consequences for the whole team.
nat: You should think about the consequences before you decide.

mis.bad: In consequence of the rain, we stayed home.
mis.good: Because of the rain, we stayed home.
mis.why: 'In consequence of' is very formal; in everyday English use 'because of' or 'as a result of'.

def: Causing a lot of public disagreement.
ex: The mayor's plan to close the road is very controversial.
nat: He is known for making controversial remarks on TV.

mis.bad: It was a very polemic decision.
mis.good: It was a very controversial decision.
mis.why: 'Polemic' is rare; the normal adjective is controversial.

def: To try to deal with a difficult problem.
ex: The government must act now to tackle climate change.
nat: We need to tackle this problem before it gets worse.

mis.bad: We need to tackle with this problem.
mis.good: We need to tackle this problem.
mis.why: 'Tackle' is transitive; no 'with'.

def: Considering everything or everyone as a whole.
ex: Overall, the trip was a great success, despite the rain.
nat: Overall, I think the new system works better than the old one.

mis.bad: In overall, I liked the film.
mis.good: Overall, I liked the film.
mis.why: Say 'overall' alone, or 'on the whole'; not 'in overall'.

def: In a way that is very sudden or very large.
ex: Prices have risen dramatically over the last two years.
nat: Her life changed dramatically after she moved abroad.

mis.bad: The weather changed dramatic.
mis.good: The weather changed dramatically.
mis.why: Use the adverb 'dramatically' to modify a verb.

def: Neat, with everything in its proper place.
ex: She keeps her room very tidy.
nat: Please tidy up your toys before dinner.

mis.bad: My room is very organizate.
mis.good: My room is very tidy.
mis.why: For a clean, neat room use tidy, not organized.

def: A little angry because something bothers you.
ex: He was annoyed because his flatmate never washed the dishes.
nat: I get annoyed when people talk loudly in the cinema.

mis.bad: I am annoying with my brother.
mis.good: I am annoyed with my brother.
mis.why: -ed describes the feeling; -ing describes what causes it.

def: To make someone agree to do something by giving reasons.
ex: It took an hour, but I finally persuaded my boss to let me work from home.
nat: She tried to persuade him to apply for the job, but he said no.

mis.bad: I persuaded that he was right.
mis.good: I convinced him that he was right.
mis.why: Persuade is for getting someone to act (persuade him to leave); for belief with "that", use convince.

def: To make someone believe that something is true.
ex: Her honest speech convinced me that the project was worth the risk.
nat: I'm not convinced this is the best plan.

mis.bad: I am convinced of that he is right.
mis.good: I am convinced that he is right.
mis.why: Use "convinced of + noun" or "convinced that + clause", never "of that".

def: To suggest something without saying it directly.
ex: I don't mean to imply that you made a mistake, but let's check the numbers.
nat: Her silence seemed to imply that she disagreed.

mis.bad: The job implies me to travel a lot.
mis.good: The job involves a lot of travel.
mis.why: Portuguese "implicar" often means "involve"; English "imply" means to suggest something indirectly.

def: To show that something is especially important.
ex: The teacher emphasized that the exam would cover the whole book.
nat: I want to emphasize how much your help means to us.

mis.bad: She emphasized on the deadline.
mis.good: She emphasized the deadline.
mis.why: Emphasize is transitive: no "on" after it.

def: To say firmly that something must happen or is true.
ex: He insisted on paying for dinner, even though we had agreed to split it.
nat: My sister insists that she locked the door.

mis.bad: He insisted me to stay.
mis.good: He insisted that I stay.
mis.why: After insist, use "on + -ing" or "that + clause", not object + "to".

def: To stop someone while they are speaking or doing something.
ex: Please don't interrupt me while I'm explaining the problem.
nat: Sorry to interrupt, but your taxi is here.

mis.bad: Don't interrupt to me.
mis.good: Don't interrupt me.
mis.why: Interrupt is transitive: no "to" before the person.

def: To pause before doing or saying something because you are unsure.
ex: Don't hesitate to call me if anything goes wrong during the trip.
nat: He hesitated for a moment before answering the question.

mis.bad: Don't hesitate in calling me.
mis.good: Don't hesitate to call me.
mis.why: Hesitate is followed by "to + verb".

def: To communicate an idea or feeling clearly.
ex: It's hard to convey how grateful I am for everything you did.
nat: The photo conveys the loneliness of the city at night.

mis.bad: I want to convey my ideas for the audience.
mis.good: I want to convey my ideas to the audience.
mis.why: Convey takes "to" before the receiver.

def: Fair, sensible, or not extreme.
ex: The restaurant serves excellent food at reasonable prices.
nat: It's reasonable to expect an answer within a week.

mis.bad: The movie was reasonable, nothing special.
mis.good: The movie was okay, nothing special.
mis.why: Portuguese "razoável" can mean "so-so"; English "reasonable" means fair or sensible.

def: Speaking in a very direct way that may sound rude.
ex: To be blunt, your presentation needs a lot more work.
nat: My grandfather is blunt, but he always tells the truth.

mis.bad: He was very blunt to me.
mis.good: He was very blunt with me.
mis.why: Use "blunt with" a person or "blunt about" a topic.

def: Careful not to upset people when you speak.
ex: She gave a tactful answer so that nobody felt offended.
nat: It wasn't very tactful to ask her age.

mis.bad: She was very tactic when she told him.
mis.good: She was very tactful when she told him.
mis.why: "Tactic" is a plan (tática); the adjective for careful, polite behavior is "tactful".

def: Not clear or exact.
ex: His instructions were so vague that nobody knew what to do.
nat: I have a vague memory of meeting her years ago.

mis.bad: He was vague in the details.
mis.good: He was vague about the details.
mis.why: Use "vague about" a topic.

def: Saying the opposite of what you mean to mock or annoy someone.
ex: Don't be so sarcastic; I'm trying to help you.
nat: He made a sarcastic comment about my new haircut.

mis.bad: It was sarcastic that the fire station burned down.
mis.good: It was ironic that the fire station burned down.
mis.why: Sarcastic describes a mocking tone; for an unexpected situation use "ironic".

def: Saying what you think openly, even if people disagree.
ex: She is an outspoken critic of the new tax policy.
nat: My aunt is very outspoken at family dinners.

mis.bad: My brother is very outspoken; he loves parties and meeting people.
mis.good: My brother is very outgoing; he loves parties and meeting people.
mis.why: Outspoken means openly giving strong opinions, not being sociable (extrovertido = outgoing).

def: A reason you give for disagreeing with something.
ex: Does anyone have an objection to moving the meeting to Friday?
nat: There was a strong objection from the neighbors.

mis.bad: I have no objection about the plan.
mis.good: I have no objection to the plan.
mis.why: Objection is followed by "to".

def: A particular way of thinking about a subject.
ex: From my viewpoint, working fewer hours would improve productivity.
nat: It helps to see the problem from another viewpoint.

mis.bad: In my point of view, the plan is bad.
mis.good: From my point of view, the plan is bad.
mis.why: Use "from my point of view", not "in my point of view".

def: A kind remark that shows you admire something.
ex: She gave me a nice compliment about my presentation.
nat: Thank you for the compliment; it made my day.

mis.bad: I did a compliment to him.
mis.good: I paid him a compliment.
mis.why: The natural verbs are "pay" or "give", not "do".

def: A story people share that may not be true.
ex: There is a rumor that the company will close next year.
nat: I don't believe rumors until I see proof.

mis.bad: People are rumoring that he is leaving.
mis.good: There is a rumor that he is leaving. / He is rumored to be leaving.
mis.why: Rumor is mainly a noun; the verb is used only in the passive ("is rumored to").

def: Giving a wrong idea of something.
ex: The advertisement was misleading because it hid the extra fees.
nat: The title is misleading; the book is about cooking.

mis.bad: The ad was mislead.
mis.good: The ad was misleading.
mis.why: Use -ing for the thing that gives a wrong idea; "misled" is the past of mislead (people are misled).

def: To say something again using different words.
ex: Let me rephrase the question so it's easier to answer.
nat: Could you rephrase that? I didn't quite follow.

mis.bad: Can you repeat in other words?
mis.good: Can you rephrase that?
mis.why: Natural ways to ask are "rephrase that" or "put it another way".

def: Money given to a student to pay for education.
ex: She won a scholarship to study engineering in Canada.
nat: He studied in London on a full scholarship.

mis.bad: She studies in a scholarship in Canada.
mis.good: She studies in Canada on a scholarship.
mis.why: A scholarship is financial aid, not a school.

def: The subjects taught in a school or course.
ex: Financial education should be part of the school curriculum.
nat: The new curriculum includes more practical projects.

mis.bad: Send me your curriculum for the job.
mis.good: Send me your resume (or CV) for the job.
mis.why: Curriculum means the courses of study; for a job use "resume" or "CV".

def: Money paid for teaching, especially at a university.
ex: Tuition at private universities has increased every year.
nat: My parents helped me pay the tuition during my first year.

mis.bad: I pay the tuition of English every day.
mis.good: I pay tuition fees for the course.
mis.why: Tuition is the money paid, not the lessons themselves.

def: To officially join a course or school.
ex: I enrolled in an evening course to improve my English.
nat: She enrolled her son in a nearby school.

mis.bad: I matriculated in a course.
mis.good: I enrolled in a course.
mis.why: "Matriculate" is rare in English; use "enroll".

def: A piece of work given to a student or employee.
ex: I have to finish this assignment before midnight.
nat: Our first assignment was to interview a stranger.

mis.bad: I have a work to deliver tomorrow.
mis.good: I have an assignment due tomorrow.
mis.why: "Work" is uncountable; a school or job task is an "assignment".

def: A skill, degree, or exam result needed for a job.
ex: You need a teaching qualification to work in a public school.
nat: Experience matters more than qualifications in this field.

mis.bad: She has many qualifications as a person, very kind.
mis.good: She has the right qualifications for the job.
mis.why: Qualifications are formal skills or certificates, not personal qualities.

def: A short period of work experience, often for students.
ex: He got an internship at a bank during the summer.
nat: Her internship turned into a full-time job.

mis.bad: I made an internship in a bank.
mis.good: I did an internship at a bank.
mis.why: Use "do" an internship, not "make".

def: A job that is available and needs someone to fill it.
ex: The company has a vacancy for a sales assistant.
nat: There are no vacancies at the moment, but we keep CVs on file.

mis.bad: There is a vague at the bank.
mis.good: There is a vacancy at the bank.
mis.why: "Vague" means unclear; a job opening is a "vacancy".

def: Moving to a higher position at work.
ex: After five years, she finally got a promotion to manager.
nat: He's hoping for a promotion before the end of the year.

mis.bad: These shoes are in promotion.
mis.good: These shoes are on sale.
mis.why: "Promotion" at work means a higher position; a lower price is "on sale".

def: To officially leave your job.
ex: He resigned after the company ignored his complaints.
nat: She resigned from her post as head teacher last week.

mis.bad: I asked for dismissal from my job.
mis.good: I resigned from my job.
mis.why: "Dismissal" means being fired; to leave voluntarily, use "resign" or "quit".

def: To stop working permanently, usually because of age.
ex: My father plans to retire when he turns sixty-five.
nat: Many people retire earlier than they expected.

mis.bad: He retired the money from the bank.
mis.good: He took the money out of the bank.
mis.why: "Retire" means to stop working; it does not mean to take something out.

def: An experienced person who gives advice to a less experienced one.
ex: My mentor taught me how to handle difficult clients.
nat: She has been a mentor to many young engineers.

mis.bad: She mentors me since 2020.
mis.good: She has been mentoring me since 2020.
mis.why: With "since" use the present perfect (continuous), not the simple present.

def: Having the skills needed to do something well.
ex: She is a competent engineer who rarely makes mistakes.
nat: You need a competent lawyer for a case like this.

mis.bad: The market is very competent.
mis.good: The market is very competitive.
mis.why: Competent means skilled; "competitive" relates to competition.

def: Giving you satisfaction because it is worthwhile.
ex: Teaching is tiring, but it is also incredibly rewarding.
nat: Volunteering at the shelter was a rewarding experience.

mis.bad: The trip was rewarded.
mis.good: The trip was rewarding.
mis.why: "Rewarded" means given a prize; -ing describes an experience that satisfies you.

def: A university student studying for a first degree.
ex: As an undergraduate, he spent a year studying abroad.
nat: Most undergraduates live on campus in their first year.

mis.bad: I'm a graduate student; I'm in my second year of a bachelor's.
mis.good: I'm an undergraduate; I'm in my second year of a bachelor's.
mis.why: In US English, a graduate student is doing a master's or PhD; a bachelor's student is an undergraduate.

def: Harmful substances that damage air, water, or land.
ex: Air pollution is a serious problem in many big cities.
nat: Plastic pollution is killing sea animals around the world.

mis.bad: The pollution of the air is high.
mis.good: Air pollution is high.
mis.why: English uses the noun adjunct "air pollution" instead of "pollution of the air".

def: A large place where rubbish is buried.
ex: Most of our household waste ends up in a landfill.
nat: The old landfill outside town will close next year.

mis.bad: The garbage goes to the sanitary landfill.
mis.good: The garbage goes to a landfill.
mis.why: "Sanitary landfill" is a technical term; in everyday English just say "landfill".

def: Animals and plants living in natural conditions.
ex: The reserve protects wildlife from illegal hunting.
nat: We saw amazing wildlife on our safari.

mis.bad: The wildlifes of Brazil are diverse.
mis.good: The wildlife of Brazil is diverse.
mis.why: Wildlife is uncountable and has no plural.

def: At risk of disappearing completely.
ex: The golden lion tamarin is an endangered species.
nat: Many endangered animals live in this rainforest.

mis.bad: It is an extinction animal.
mis.good: It is an endangered animal.
mis.why: "Extinct" means already gone; an animal at risk is "endangered".

def: Able to continue without harming the environment.
ex: The company aims to use only sustainable materials by 2030.
nat: Fast fashion is not a sustainable way to dress.

mis.bad: It is a sustentable project.
mis.good: It is a sustainable project.
mis.why: The English form is "sustainable", not "sustentable".

def: Gases or substances released into the air.
ex: The city wants to cut carbon emissions by half within ten years.
nat: Car emissions are a major source of air pollution.

mis.bad: The emission of carbon is rising.
mis.good: Carbon emissions are rising.
mis.why: Use the plural "emissions" with a noun adjunct.

def: A long period with very little rain.
ex: The drought destroyed most of the crops last summer.
nat: Farmers are struggling after three years of drought.

mis.bad: The drought is a hot day.
mis.good: The drought lasted three months.
mis.why: Drought means a long lack of rain, not hot weather.

def: The cutting down of large areas of forest.
ex: Deforestation in the Amazon has slowed down in recent years.
nat: Illegal logging is the main cause of deforestation here.

mis.bad: The deforestation is growing in the Amazon.
mis.good: Deforestation is growing in the Amazon.
mis.why: No article before a general uncountable noun.

def: An unfair difference in wealth or opportunity.
ex: Income inequality has grown in many countries.
nat: The report highlights inequality in access to education.

mis.bad: The inequalities is big in Brazil.
mis.good: Inequality is big in Brazil.
mis.why: In this sense, inequality is usually uncountable.

def: The state of being very poor.
ex: Millions of people still live in poverty.
nat: She grew up in poverty but became a successful doctor.

mis.bad: They live in the poverty.
mis.good: They live in poverty.
mis.why: No article before "poverty" in this sense.

def: To offer to do something without being paid or forced.
ex: I volunteer at an animal shelter every Saturday.
nat: Nobody volunteered to clean the kitchen.

mis.bad: I made a voluntary work at the school.
mis.good: I do volunteer work at the school.
mis.why: Use "do volunteer work", not "make voluntary work".

def: To give money or goods to help others.
ex: Many people donated clothes after the flood.
nat: He donates part of his salary to charity every month.

mis.bad: She donated the charity some money.
mis.good: She donated some money to the charity.
mis.why: Donate cannot take two objects; use "to".

def: Unfair treatment of people because of who they are.
ex: The law bans discrimination based on age or gender.
nat: Many workers face discrimination because of their accent.

mis.bad: There is a lot of discrimination to women.
mis.good: There is a lot of discrimination against women.
mis.why: The preposition is "against".

def: The state of having no job.
ex: Youth unemployment is a major concern in the region.
nat: Unemployment fell to its lowest level in ten years.

mis.bad: The unemployment is high.
mis.good: Unemployment is high.
mis.why: No article before the general noun.

def: Worried and nervous about something uncertain.
ex: I felt anxious before my job interview.
nat: He is anxious about the test results.

mis.bad: I am anxious to go on vacation tomorrow.
mis.good: I am excited to go on vacation tomorrow.
mis.why: "Anxious" suggests worry, not simple excitement.

def: Having a strong wish to succeed.
ex: She is an ambitious young lawyer who wants to become a judge.
nat: They have ambitious plans to open ten new stores.

mis.bad: I am ambitious of becoming a manager.
mis.good: I am ambitious and want to become a manager.
mis.why: "Ambitious of" is not used; ambitious describes character.

def: Not confident about yourself.
ex: He felt insecure about his accent at first.
nat: Constant criticism can make anyone feel insecure.

mis.bad: I am insecure to walk at night.
mis.good: I feel unsafe walking at night.
mis.why: "Insecure" describes lack of confidence; for danger use "unsafe".

def: Showing care for other people's feelings.
ex: It was thoughtful of you to bring flowers.
nat: She sent a thoughtful message when I was sick.

mis.bad: It was very thoughtful from you.
mis.good: It was very thoughtful of you.
mis.why: Use "of you" after adjectives describing behavior (thoughtful, kind, nice).

def: Willing to give more than is expected.
ex: My uncle is generous and always pays for everyone.
nat: That's a very generous offer; thank you.

mis.bad: He is generous of money.
mis.good: He is generous with his money.
mis.why: Use "generous with" something.

def: Having moods that change quickly, often to bad ones.
ex: He gets moody when he doesn't sleep enough.
nat: Teenagers can be moody at times.

mis.bad: I am moody to travel.
mis.good: I am in the mood to travel.
mis.why: "Moody" means changeable in mood; the wish to do something is "in the mood for/to".

def: Relaxed and not easily upset.
ex: My boss is easygoing, so the office is a pleasant place.
nat: She is easygoing and gets along with everyone.

mis.bad: She is very easy going with everyone.
mis.good: She is very easygoing with everyone.
mis.why: It is one word (or hyphenated: easy-going), not two.

def: Caring only about yourself.
ex: It was selfish of him to take the last piece without asking.
nat: Don't be selfish; share your toys.

mis.bad: He is very selfish person.
mis.good: He is a very selfish person.
mis.why: Singular countable nouns need an article.

def: Not proud and not thinking you are better than others.
ex: Despite his fame, he stays humble and kind.
nat: She comes from a humble background.

mis.bad: He is very humiliated about his success.
mis.good: He is very humble about his success.
mis.why: "Humiliated" means shamed by others; "humble" (humilde) means modest.

def: Sad because something was not as good as you hoped.
ex: I was disappointed with the final episode of the series.
nat: They were disappointed that the concert was cancelled.

mis.bad: I am disappointed of you.
mis.good: I am disappointed with you.
mis.why: Use "with" or "in" after disappointed, not "of".

def: Happy because something bad did not happen.
ex: I was so relieved when the test results came back negative.
nat: She looked relieved to hear that everyone was safe.

mis.bad: I'm very relief that you are safe.
mis.good: I'm very relieved that you are safe.
mis.why: Use the adjective "relieved", not the noun "relief".

def: Feeling awkward or ashamed in front of others.
ex: I felt embarrassed when I forgot his name.
nat: He was too embarrassed to ask for help.

mis.bad: I was embarassed because I forgot his name.
mis.good: I was embarrassed because I forgot his name.
mis.why: Mind the spelling: double r and double s. Also, it never means "pregnant", unlike "embaraçada".

def: Very excited and interested in something.
ex: The students were enthusiastic about the new project.
nat: He wasn't very enthusiastic about moving to another city.

mis.bad: She is enthusiastic of the idea.
mis.good: She is enthusiastic about the idea.
mis.why: Use "about" after enthusiastic.

def: Annoyed because you have to wait or because things are slow.
ex: I get impatient when the line moves slowly.
nat: He was impatient to start the new job.

mis.bad: She is impatient for her kids.
mis.good: She is impatient with her kids.
mis.why: Use "impatient with" a person.

def: Showing that you understand and care about someone's problems.
ex: My manager was sympathetic when I explained my situation.
nat: She gave me a sympathetic smile.

mis.bad: He is very sympathetic with everybody, always smiling.
mis.good: He is very friendly with everybody, always smiling.
mis.why: "Sympathetic" means understanding of suffering; "simpático" is "nice" or "friendly".

def: To delay doing something that you should do.
ex: I always procrastinate when I have to write reports.
nat: Stop procrastinating and start your homework.

mis.bad: I procrastinated to study.
mis.good: I procrastinated instead of studying.
mis.why: Procrastinate is intransitive and is not followed by "to + verb".

def: The practice of paying full attention to the present moment.
ex: Ten minutes of mindfulness each morning helps me stay calm.
nat: She teaches mindfulness at a local clinic.

mis.bad: I practice a mindfulness every day.
mis.good: I practice mindfulness every day.
mis.why: Mindfulness is uncountable.

def: The usual way you do things every day.
ex: My morning routine includes a short walk and a cup of coffee.
nat: Travelling disrupted my sleep routine.

mis.bad: I have a busy routine of work.
mis.good: I have a busy daily routine.
mis.why: The usual phrase is "daily routine".

pt: distração, o que desvia a atenção
def: Something that takes your attention away from what you are doing.
