ex: My phone is the biggest distraction when I study.
nat: Turn off the TV; it's a distraction.

mis.bad: I am a distraction person, I forget everything.
mis.good: I am easily distracted, so I forget things.
mis.why: "Distraction" is something that diverts attention; it does not describe a personality.

def: How much you value yourself.
ex: Positive feedback can raise a child's self-esteem.
nat: Social media can damage teenagers' self-esteem.

mis.bad: I have a low self-esteem.
mis.good: I have low self-esteem.
mis.why: Self-esteem is uncountable: no article.

def: To think too much about something so that it causes stress.
ex: Stop overthinking; it was just a short message.
nat: I tend to overthink small decisions.

mis.bad: I overthink too much about everything.
mis.good: I overthink everything.
mis.why: The prefix "over-" already means "too much".

def: To relax after a period of work or stress.
ex: I like to unwind with a book after a long day.
nat: We went to the beach to unwind for the weekend.

mis.bad: I unwinded on the sofa.
mis.good: I unwound on the sofa.
mis.why: The past of unwind is irregular: unwound.

def: Extremely tired.
ex: After the long flight, I was completely exhausted.
nat: She looked exhausted after working two shifts.

mis.bad: I am exhausting after work.
mis.good: I am exhausted after work.
mis.why: Use -ed for how you feel; "exhausting" describes what causes it.

def: To say or do something that makes someone feel less worried.
ex: The doctor reassured her that the test was routine.
nat: His calm voice reassured the nervous passengers.

mis.bad: He reassured me to not worry.
mis.good: He reassured me that there was nothing to worry about.
mis.why: Reassure takes an object plus "that + clause", not "to + verb".

def: The ability to control yourself and keep doing something.
ex: Learning a language takes discipline, not just talent.
nat: He has the discipline to train every morning.

mis.bad: I study discipline English at school.
mis.good: I study English as a subject at school.
mis.why: "Discipline" means self-control or order; a school subject is better called "subject".

def: A message from an app or phone telling you something new happened.
ex: I turned off notifications so I could focus on my work.
nat: You'll get a notification when your order ships.

mis.bad: I received a notification of the app.
mis.good: I received a notification from the app.
mis.why: The sender is introduced with "from".

def: A regular payment to receive a service or product.
ex: I cancelled my streaming subscription because I never used it.
nat: A yearly subscription is cheaper than paying monthly.

mis.bad: I made a signature of the magazine.
mis.good: I took out a subscription to the magazine.
mis.why: "Signature" is a handwritten name; for a service, use "subscription".

def: Watching or listening online without downloading.
ex: Streaming has changed the way people watch films.
nat: Most of my friends use streaming services instead of cable TV.

mis.bad: I watch series in streaming.
mis.good: I watch series on a streaming service.
mis.why: English does not say "in streaming"; use "streaming service" or the verb "stream".

def: The title of a news story, usually in large letters.
ex: The headline made the story sound far worse than it was.
nat: I only read the headlines on my phone each morning.

mis.bad: The newspaper's head was misleading.
mis.good: The newspaper's headline was misleading.
mis.why: A news title is a "headline", not a "head".

def: A person who affects what others buy or do through social media.
ex: The brand paid an influencer to promote its new sneakers.
nat: My cousin wants to become a full-time influencer.

mis.bad: She is a digital influencer.
mis.good: She is a social media influencer.
mis.why: "Digital influencer" is a Portuguese pattern; English says "social media influencer" or just "influencer".

def: Spreading very quickly on the internet.
ex: The video went viral and got ten million views in a day.
nat: A viral post turned the small bakery into a local celebrity.

mis.bad: The video became viral.
mis.good: The video went viral.
mis.why: The natural collocation is "go viral".

def: Making you want to do or use something again and again.
ex: This game is so addictive that I lose track of time.
nat: Sugar can be as addictive as some drugs, researchers say.

mis.bad: This game is very vicious.
mis.good: This game is very addictive.
mis.why: "Viciante" is "addictive"; "vicious" means cruel or violent.

def: False information shared without necessarily meaning to deceive.
ex: Misinformation spread quickly during the election.
nat: Always check the source to avoid sharing misinformation.

mis.bad: There are many misinformations online.
mis.good: There is a lot of misinformation online.
mis.why: Misinformation is uncountable.

def: To move text or images up and down on a screen.
ex: I scrolled through my feed for an hour without noticing.
nat: Scroll down to see the full list of prices.

mis.bad: I made scroll on the page.
mis.good: I scrolled down the page.
mis.why: Scroll is a verb itself; do not use "make scroll".

def: To look at things online or in a shop without a fixed aim.
ex: I browsed the website for an hour before buying anything.
nat: I like to browse in bookstores on Saturdays.

mis.bad: I navigate on the internet every night.
mis.good: I browse the internet every night.
mis.why: "Navigate" is for finding your way; for casual web use, say "browse".

def: A small problem that stops something from working properly.
ex: A software glitch delayed all flights this morning.
nat: There was a glitch in the video, so it kept freezing.

mis.bad: The system had a glitch of connection.
mis.good: The system had a connection glitch.
mis.why: Put the noun before "glitch" (a connection glitch) instead of using "of".

def: To disconnect a device from the power, or to take a break from technology.
ex: I unplugged the router and waited a minute before restarting it.
nat: We go to a cabin every summer to unplug from our phones.

mis.bad: Please unplug the light.
mis.good: Please turn off the light.
mis.why: Unplug means to pull a plug from a socket; lights are turned off.

def: The control of what people can say, read, or see.
ex: The government introduced strict censorship of the press.
nat: Online censorship makes it hard to get honest news.

mis.bad: There is a censorship in that country.
mis.good: There is censorship in that country.
mis.why: Censorship is uncountable.

def: A person who writes or reports news.
ex: The journalist interviewed several witnesses about the accident.
nat: My sister is a journalist for a local newspaper.

mis.bad: She works as a journalist in the journal of the city.
mis.good: She works as a journalist for the city newspaper.
mis.why: False friend: "journal" is a specialist or academic publication; a daily is a "newspaper" (jornal).

def: To give money to support an event or team in return for advertising.
ex: A local bank sponsors the youth football team.
nat: The festival is sponsored by several large companies.

mis.bad: The company patronizes the festival.
mis.good: The company sponsors the festival.
mis.why: "Patronize" means to treat someone as inferior; use "sponsor" for funding.

def: To watch and direct people or work to make sure it is done well.
ex: She supervises a team of twelve technicians.
nat: A teacher must supervise the students on the trip.

mis.bad: I supervise to the team.
mis.good: I supervise the team.
mis.why: Supervise is transitive, with no preposition.

def: To organize different people or tasks so they work well together.
ex: Someone has to coordinate the schedules of all the speakers.
nat: He coordinates volunteers at the city's food bank.

mis.bad: She coordinates to the project.
mis.good: She coordinates the project.
mis.why: Coordinate is transitive; use "coordinate with" only for working together with someone.

def: To produce many ideas quickly in a group.
ex: We brainstormed names for the new product for an hour.
nat: Let's brainstorm some solutions before the meeting ends.

mis.bad: We made a brainstorm to find ideas.
mis.good: We brainstormed ideas.
mis.why: Brainstorm is mainly a verb; as a noun say "brainstorming session".

def: Comments about how well someone is doing.
ex: My manager gave me useful feedback on the report.
nat: We welcome feedback from our customers.

mis.bad: I got many feedbacks from my boss.
mis.good: I got a lot of feedback from my boss.
mis.why: Feedback is uncountable.

def: To work together to achieve something.
ex: The two departments need to cooperate to solve this issue.
nat: The suspect refused to cooperate with the police.

mis.bad: We cooperate to each other.
mis.good: We cooperate with each other.
mis.why: Cooperate takes "with".

def: An opinion that all members of a group agree on.
ex: After a long discussion, the team reached a consensus.
nat: There is no consensus among scientists on this issue.

mis.bad: We made a consensus.
mis.good: We reached a consensus.
mis.why: The collocation is "reach" (or "build") a consensus.

def: The ability to start something without being told.
ex: She took the initiative and organized the training herself.
nat: He shows a lot of initiative for a new employee.

mis.bad: She made the initiative to start the project.
mis.good: She took the initiative to start the project.
mis.why: Use "take the initiative", not "make".

def: To make someone want to do something.
ex: A good leader knows how to motivate the team.
nat: Money alone doesn't motivate most people.

mis.bad: She is very motivate.
mis.good: She is very motivated.
mis.why: Use the adjective "motivated".

def: To give people the confidence or authority to make decisions.
ex: Good managers empower their staff to solve problems on their own.
nat: The program empowers women to start their own businesses.

mis.bad: The company empowers to employees.
mis.good: The company empowers employees.
mis.why: Empower is transitive: no "to" before the object.

def: To control every small detail of other people's work.
ex: Our boss micromanages everything, so nobody feels trusted.
nat: I hate it when someone micromanages me.

mis.bad: My boss is very micromanage.
mis.good: My boss is a micromanager.
mis.why: Micromanage is a verb; the person is a "micromanager".

def: Praise or credit given for good work.
ex: She finally received recognition for her years of hard work.
nat: Employees need recognition to stay motivated.

mis.bad: He got recognition of the boss.
mis.good: He got recognition from the boss.
mis.why: Use "from" for the source of the recognition.

def: To weaken something gradually.
ex: Constant gossip can undermine trust within a team.
nat: His rude comments undermined my confidence.

mis.bad: Gossip undermines to the team.
mis.good: Gossip undermines the team.
mis.why: Undermine is transitive: no preposition before the object.

def: To give something, such as ideas or money, to help achieve something.
ex: Everyone contributed ideas during the workshop.
nat: Stress contributes to many health problems.

mis.bad: He contributed for the project.
mis.good: He contributed to the project.
mis.why: Use "to" after contribute.

def: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other.
ex: The new coach quickly built rapport with the players.
nat: Good rapport with clients can lead to repeat business.

mis.bad: I have a good rapport of him.
mis.good: I have a good rapport with him.
mis.why: Use "rapport with" a person.

def: A serious disagreement between people or groups.
ex: The two neighbors are in a long dispute over the fence.
nat: A pay dispute led to a strike at the factory.

mis.bad: The two teams are in a dispute for the title.
mis.good: The two teams are competing for the title.
mis.why: "Disputa" can mean competition; English "dispute" is a disagreement or argument.

def: A piece of paper that shows you paid for something.
ex: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the shirt.
nat: Can I have the receipt, please?

mis.bad: Can you give me the recipe of the purchase?
mis.good: Can I have the receipt?
mis.why: Recipe is for cooking; the paper for a purchase is a receipt.

def: A lower price than normal.
ex: They gave us a ten percent discount for paying in cash.
nat: Students get a discount at the cinema.

mis.bad: They made a discount of ten percent to me.
mis.good: They gave me a ten percent discount.
mis.why: The natural verbs are "give" or "offer" a discount.

def: A promise by a company to repair a product if it breaks.
ex: The laptop comes with a two-year warranty.
nat: The warranty expired last month, so we have to pay for repairs.

mis.bad: The product has a garantee of two years.
mis.good: The product has a two-year warranty.
mis.why: For a product, "warranty" is more common than "guarantee".

def: A person who takes payment in a shop.
ex: The cashier gave me the wrong change.
nat: Please pay the cashier on your way out.

mis.bad: I paid in the cashier.
mis.good: I paid the cashier.
mis.why: You pay a person; at the till you say "at the checkout".

def: Costing more than it is worth.
ex: The food was good but overpriced for such a small portion.
nat: I think these sneakers are overpriced.

mis.bad: This shirt is too much expensive.
mis.good: This shirt is overpriced.
mis.why: "Too much" is not used before an adjective; say "too expensive" or "overpriced".

def: A person who owns a property and rents it to others.
ex: Our landlord is fixing the heating this week.
nat: I pay my rent to the landlord on the first of each month.

mis.bad: My proprietary raised the rent.
mis.good: My landlord raised the rent.
mis.why: "Proprietary" means owned by a company; the person who rents out a home is a "landlord".

def: A person who pays rent to live in or use a property.
ex: The tenant complained about the broken elevator.
nat: The tenants have to leave by the end of June.

mis.bad: He is a tenent in my building.
mis.good: He is a tenant in my building.
mis.why: Spelling: tenant ends in -ant.

def: To pay money regularly to use a house, flat, or car.
ex: We rent a small apartment close to the subway.
nat: Many young people can't afford to buy a house, so they rent.

mis.bad: The rent of a car costs a lot.
mis.good: Renting a car costs a lot.
mis.why: As a noun, "rent" is the regular payment for housing; for the action use the verb or "car rental".

def: Having furniture already inside.
ex: They found a furnished apartment near the university.
nat: The flat is fully furnished, so you only need to bring clothes.

mis.bad: I'm looking for a furnitured apartment.
mis.good: I'm looking for a furnished apartment.
mis.why: The adjective is "furnished" (from furnish), not "furnitured".

def: To repair and improve an old building.
ex: They renovated the old house before moving in.
nat: We plan to renovate the kitchen next spring.

mis.bad: I am doing a reform in my house.
mis.good: I am renovating my house.
mis.why: "Reform" in English means to change laws or behavior, not to renovate a building.

def: A machine used at home, such as a fridge or washing machine.
ex: Most kitchen appliances are cheaper during the holiday sales.
nat: This appliance uses a lot of electricity.

mis.bad: I bought a new electrodomestic.
mis.good: I bought a new appliance.
mis.why: The English word is "appliance".

def: A part of a town where people live.
ex: It is a quiet neighborhood with lots of parks.
nat: We moved to a nicer neighborhood last year.

mis.bad: I live in the neighborhood Savassi.
mis.good: I live in the Savassi neighborhood.
mis.why: English puts the name before "neighborhood"; Portuguese puts "bairro" first.

def: An area outside the center of a city where people live.
ex: They live in a green suburb about twenty minutes from downtown.
nat: Many families move to the suburbs for more space.

mis.bad: I live in a poor suburb with no buildings.
mis.good: I live in a suburb outside the city.
mis.why: In English, suburbs are often comfortable residential areas, not necessarily poor.

def: A person walking rather than driving.
ex: A car hit a pedestrian near the crossing.
nat: The street is closed to traffic and open only to pedestrians.

mis.bad: The pedestrian cross is closed.
mis.good: The pedestrian crossing is closed.
mis.why: The phrase is "pedestrian crossing" (US: crosswalk).

def: In or toward the main business area of a city.
ex: I work downtown, so I take the subway every day.
nat: We went downtown for dinner and a movie.

mis.bad: I live in the downtown of the city.
mis.good: I live downtown.
mis.why: "Downtown" is usually an adverb or adjective in American English.

def: More and more as time goes on.
ex: Increasingly, cities are banning single-use plastic bags.
nat: Remote work is increasingly common in my industry.

mis.bad: Each time more people work from home.
mis.good: Increasingly, more people work from home.
mis.why: "Cada vez mais" is "increasingly" or "more and more", not "each time more".

def: The state of having more than one possible meaning or being open to multiple interpretations.
ex: There is some ambiguity in the contract regarding payment terms.
nat: Clear documentation reduces ambiguity across distributed teams.

mis.bad: The text has double sense.
mis.good: The text is ambiguous / has some ambiguity.
mis.why: In English, "double sense" is a false friend for "duplo sentido"; use ambiguity or double meaning.

def: Possible to do easily or conveniently.
ex: The architect confirmed that the project is technically feasible.
nat: Given our current budget, this solution seems much more feasible.

mis.bad: This project is very viabilized.
mis.good: This project is very feasible.
mis.why: English does not use "viabilize"; use feasible or viable.

def: Including or dealing with all or nearly all elements or aspects of something.
ex: We conducted a comprehensive review of all company policies.
nat: The onboarding guide gives new hires a comprehensive overview of the product.

mis.bad: He is very comprehensive with my mistakes.
mis.good: He is very understanding of my mistakes.
mis.why: False friend: "comprehensive" means broad/inclusive; "compreensivo" is understanding.

def: A person or thing holding a corresponding position or performing a similar function in another place.
ex: The Brazilian CEO met with her European counterpart in Paris.
nat: I often coordinate features with my counterparts in the design department.

mis.bad: My homologue in the US team agreed.
mis.good: My counterpart in the US team agreed.
mis.why: "Homologue" is rare/technical; in business and professional English, use "counterpart".

def: Showing no activity, growth, or development.
ex: Wages have remained stagnant despite rising inflation.
nat: Without innovation, products quickly become stagnant in competitive markets.

mis.bad: The career became stopped.
mis.good: My career became stagnant.
mis.why: Use "stagnant" to describe lack of economic or career growth.

def: Critical observation or examination.
ex: Public figures face intense scrutiny from the press and social media.
nat: Every line of security code underwent strict scrutiny before release.

mis.bad: The code passed for a big verification.
mis.good: The code came under close scrutiny.
mis.why: "Under scrutiny" is the high-level natural idiom for rigorous inspection.

def: Able to adapt or be adapted to many different functions or activities.
ex: Python is a versatile programming language used for both web dev and data science.
nat: She is a versatile professional who handles both sales and engineering calls.

mis.bad: He is very polivalent in his job.
mis.good: He is very versatile in his job.
mis.why: "Polivalente" translates naturally as "versatile" or "multiskilled", not polivalent.

def: A lack of compatibility or similarity between two or more facts or numbers.
ex: The auditor found a discrepancy between the receipts and bank statements.
nat: There was a noticeable discrepancy between what was promised and what was delivered.

mis.bad: There was a divergence in the accounts.
mis.good: There was a discrepancy in the accounts.
mis.why: When accounting numbers or metrics do not match, use "discrepancy".

def: Strict, precise, and exacting (of regulations, requirements, or conditions).
ex: Aviation security is subject to stringent international regulations.
nat: Our team adheres to stringent data protection policies.

mis.bad: The company has very rigid laws.
mis.good: The company has stringent rules / regulations.
mis.why: For compliance, laws, and professional standards, "stringent" is the idiomatic B2+/C1 adjective.

def: Denoting an action or event preceding or preparing for something fuller or more important.
ex: Preliminary results suggest the vaccine is both safe and effective.
nat: We had a preliminary discussion before presenting the proposal to stakeholders.

mis.bad: We made a preview analysis.
mis.good: We conducted a preliminary analysis.
mis.why: "Preview" is a sneak peek or trailer; for early phases of analysis/results, use "preliminary".

def: Combine a number of things into a single more effective whole, or make something firmer.
ex: The merger helped the tech startup consolidate its market position.
nat: We decided to consolidate all our cloud servers into one unified platform.

mis.bad: We joined all databases in one.
mis.good: We consolidated all databases into one.
mis.why: In professional and tech environments, use "consolidate" for merging disparate systems.

def: Never done or known before.
ex: The tech sector experienced unprecedented growth during the digital boom.
nat: Facing an unprecedented surge in server traffic, our engineers worked around the clock.

mis.bad: It was a thing never seen before in history.
mis.good: It was an unprecedented event.
mis.why: "Unprecedented" is concise, elegant, and native for historic first-time occurrences.

def: Become progressively worse in quality or condition.
ex: Customer relations began to deteriorate after the prolonged service outage.
nat: Without regular updates, software performance will gradually deteriorate.

mis.bad: The situation was getting more bad.
mis.good: The situation was deteriorating / getting worse.
mis.why: "More bad" is grammatically incorrect; use "deteriorate" for formal progressive decline.

def: So delicate or precise as to be difficult to analyze or describe; not obvious.
ex: There is a subtle difference in meaning between these two English words.
nat: Good UI designers pay attention to subtle cues like animations and spacing.

mis.bad: The "b" is pronounced in subtle.
mis.good: Pronounce it /ˈsʌt.əl/ — the "b" is silent!
mis.why: Crucial pronunciation trap: "subtle" is pronounced /SUT-ul/, the "b" is completely silent.

def: Seeming reasonable, probable, or believable.
ex: The engineer offered a plausible explanation for why the database had crashed.
nat: His theory sounds plausible, but we need hard metrics to confirm it.

mis.bad: That makes sense so it is possible true.
mis.good: That explanation is entirely plausible.
mis.why: "Plausible" specifically denotes an explanation or claim that sounds believable and likely.

def: Certain to happen; unavoidable.
ex: With the company expanding so fast, hiring more managers was inevitable.
nat: Change is inevitable in technology; adaptability is what keeps businesses alive.

mis.bad: It was without escape.
mis.good: It was inevitable.
mis.why: Use "inevitable" to express events that could not be prevented or avoided.

def: Producing a great deal of profit.
ex: Cloud consulting has turned into an extremely lucrative industry.
nat: She left her corporate role after landing several lucrative freelance contracts.

mis.bad: It is a very profitable contract (not wrong, but lucrative adds nuance).
mis.good: It is a highly lucrative contract.
mis.why: "Lucrative" emphasizes generating substantial wealth or financial returns.

def: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically in a way that is based on practical rather than theoretical considerations.
ex: Instead of searching for a perfect solution, the tech lead took a pragmatic approach.
nat: Good managers strike a balance between visionary ideals and pragmatic execution.

mis.bad: He is very practical (often misses the nuance of realistic problem-solving).
mis.good: He took a pragmatic stance on the budget cut.
mis.why: "Pragmatic" implies making realistic decisions despite constraints or imperfect conditions.

def: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially for the worse.
ex: Cryptocurrency markets are notoriously volatile and carry high risk.
nat: In a volatile macroeconomic environment, companies build cash reserves.

mis.bad: The prices are very instable.
mis.good: The prices are highly volatile.
mis.why: "Instable" is incorrect in standard English; use "unstable" or "volatile".

def: Perceptible by touch, or clear and definite; real.
ex: We need to see tangible results before investing additional capital.
nat: Automating customer support delivered tangible cost savings within three months.

mis.bad: We want to see concrete proofs.
mis.good: We want to see tangible evidence / results.
mis.why: In English, evidence is uncountable, and "tangible results" is the standard business collocation.

def: A difficult or unpleasant situation or state of misfortune.
ex: Great leaders inspire confidence and resilience in times of adversity.
nat: Overcoming adversity early in life shaped her entrepreneurial determination.

mis.bad: She suffered many bad lucks.
mis.good: She faced severe adversity.
mis.why: "Luck" is uncountable; use "adversity" or "misfortune" to express serious hardship.

def: A future event or circumstance which is possible but cannot be predicted with certainty.
ex: Every major launch should have a contingency plan in case of outage.
nat: We allocated 10% of the project budget for unexpected contingencies.

mis.bad: We need a emergency plan B.
mis.good: We need a contingency plan.
mis.why: "Contingency plan" is the professional B2/C1 standard term in engineering and management.

def: A typical example or pattern of something; a distinct set of concepts or thought patterns.
ex: Cloud computing triggered a fundamental paradigm shift in enterprise software.
nat: Microservices represent a different architectural paradigm from monolithic apps.

mis.bad: The "g" is sounded: /paradig-m/.
mis.good: Pronounce it /ˈper.ə.daɪm/ — the "g" is silent!
mis.why: Pronunciation trap: "paradigm" rhymes with time/dime; never pronounce the "g".

def: Held or arrived at by the agreement of all people involved.
ex: The board was unanimous in its decision to approve the acquisition.
nat: After an intense debate, the committee reached a unanimous agreement.

mis.bad: The decision was unanimated.
mis.good: The decision was unanimous.
mis.why: False friend: "unanimated" means without life/spirit; "unânime" is unanimous.

def: Becoming more and more rapid (of an increase).
ex: Mobile adoption experienced exponential growth over the past decade.
nat: AI computing power has expanded at an exponential rate in recent years.

mis.bad: The user count grew in exponent.
mis.good: The user count grew exponentially.
mis.why: Use the adverb "exponentially" or the adjective "exponential growth".

def: A thing that motivates or encourages someone to do something.
ex: Annual performance bonuses provide a strong financial incentive for salespeople.
nat: Tax incentives have encouraged many green energy startups to open factories here.

mis.bad: The company gave an incentivization.
mis.good: The company offered an incentive.
mis.why: In English, use the noun "incentive" rather than "incentivization".

pt: concessão mútua, compromisso, escolha entre vantagens
def: A balance achieved between two desirable but incompatible features; a compromise.
ex: In software development, there is often a trade-off between speed and code quality.
nat: Choosing remote work involves a trade-off between flexibility and face-to-face networking.

mis.bad: We have to make a concession between speed and cost.
mis.good: We have to evaluate the trade-off between speed and cost.
mis.why: When choosing between two desirable engineering or life attributes, use "trade-off".

def: A subtle difference in or shade of meaning, expression, or sound.
ex: At an advanced level of English, understanding nuance is vital for diplomatic communication.
nat: Machine translation often misses the cultural nuances of colloquial speech.

mis.bad: The text has delicate tones of sense.
mis.good: The text captures subtle nuances of meaning.
mis.why: "Nuance" is the precise term for subtle shades of meaning or tone.

def: Widespread in a particular area or at a particular time.
ex: Burnout is increasingly prevalent among technology professionals working remote hours.
nat: The belief that multitasking boosts productivity is still prevalent despite research.

mis.bad: This behavior is very predominant in society.
mis.good: This behavior is prevalent in society.
mis.why: "Prevalent" is natural when describing widespread habits, illnesses, or beliefs.

def: Logical and consistent; able to speak clearly and logically.
ex: The candidate presented a coherent strategy for growing the company revenue.
nat: After an all-night coding sprint, he was barely coherent during the morning meeting.

mis.bad: The explanation was without connection.
mis.good: The explanation was not coherent / lacked coherence.
mis.why: Use "coherent" for arguments, texts, or speech that follow clear logic.

def: Based on random choice or personal whim, rather than any reason or system.
ex: Setting a 30-day deadline without assessing the scope seemed completely arbitrary.
nat: The rules felt arbitrary because they were never clearly explained or justified.

mis.bad: He decided by head without reason.
mis.good: His decision seemed completely arbitrary.
mis.why: "Arbitrary" describes actions taken without objective rules or evidence.

def: Extremely thorough, exhaustive, or accurate.
ex: All medical equipment must pass rigorous laboratory testing before public release.
nat: The team applied rigorous benchmarks to test system load and memory usage.

mis.bad: The test was made with big rigor.
mis.good: The test was conducted with rigorous precision.
mis.why: Use the adjective "rigorous testing" or "rigorous analysis" in technical writing.

def: Not certain or fixed; provisional; done without confidence.
ex: We reached a tentative agreement, pending final approval from legal counsel.
nat: Let us set a tentative date for next Thursday and confirm early next week.

mis.bad: We marked an appointment for test.
mis.good: We scheduled a tentative meeting for Thursday.
mis.why: For business dates or agreements that are subject to confirmation, use "tentative".

def: Smooth and effortless; having or creating no impediments or resistance.
ex: Fintech apps aim to make online payments completely frictionless.
nat: Our primary design objective is delivering a frictionless onboarding experience.

mis.bad: The experience had no friction points (not wrong, but frictionless is standard).
mis.good: The user enjoyed a frictionless payment process.
mis.why: "Frictionless" is the dominant B2+/C1 tech and product term for seamless user flows.

def: Innovatively altering or destroying an existing business model or market structure.
ex: Ride-sharing proved to be a highly disruptive technology for urban transportation.
nat: Generative AI represents the most disruptive innovation of this decade.

mis.bad: It disrupted everything so it was disruptor.
mis.good: It was a highly disruptive innovation.
mis.why: Use "disruptive" as the adjective and "disruptor" as the person/company doing the disruption.

def: To distribute resources or duties for a particular purpose.
ex: We need to allocate more budget to security testing this quarter.
nat: The manager allocated three engineers to the migration.

mis.bad: We need to allocate more time for the project.
mis.good: We need to allocate more time to the project.
mis.why: Use "allocate something to" (not for) a task or recipient.

def: To make minor changes to a text, law, or agreement to improve or update it.
ex: The legal team asked us to amend two clauses in the contract.
nat: They amended the policy after receiving customer feedback.

mis.bad: We need to amend about the contract.
mis.good: We need to amend the contract.
mis.why: "Amend" is transitive and takes a direct object without "about".

def: To state a fact or belief confidently and forcefully.
ex: She asserted that the new architecture would cut latency in half.
nat: He had to assert his authority during the heated meeting.

mis.bad: She asserted to us that it was safe.
mis.good: She asserted that it was safe.
mis.why: "Assert" is normally followed directly by a "that" clause without an indirect object.

def: To give someone a particular job, task, or responsibility.
ex: The lead developer assigned the bug ticket to a junior engineer.
nat: Each participant was assigned a mentor for the program.

mis.bad: He assigned me for fixing the bug.
mis.good: He assigned me to fix the bug.
mis.why: Use "assign someone to do something" or "assign a task to someone".

def: To succeed in achieving something after effort.
ex: It took three years of steady practice to attain fluency in English.
nat: Few startups attain profitability in their first year.

mis.bad: I want to attain to B2 level.
mis.good: I want to attain B2 level.
mis.why: "Attain" takes a direct object with no "to".

def: To go around or avoid an obstacle, rule, or standard procedure.
ex: Never bypass authentication checks, even in a staging environment.
nat: We can bypass the city center by taking the ring road.

mis.bad: They bypassed from the approval process.
mis.good: They bypassed the approval process.
mis.why: "Bypass" is transitive and does not take "from".

def: To bring or come to an end.
ex: The legacy API will cease operating at the end of December.
nat: The company ceased trading after the merger.

mis.bad: The noise ceased to making sound.
mis.good: The noise ceased to bother us.
mis.why: Use "cease + -ing" or "cease + to + base verb".

def: To act in accordance with a wish, command, or set of rules.
ex: All vendors must comply with local data privacy regulations.
nat: Failure to comply with the policy will suspend your account.

mis.bad: We must comply the new rules.
mis.good: We must comply with the new rules.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "with" after "comply".

pt: comprometer / ceder para chegar a acordo
def: To settle a dispute by mutual concession, or to expose something to risk.
ex: A weak password can compromise the entire corporate network.
nat: Both sides had to compromise to sign the agreement.

mis.bad: The leak compromised with our reputation.
mis.good: The leak compromised our reputation.
mis.why: When meaning "put at risk", "compromise" takes a direct object.

def: To form or devise a plan or idea in the mind.
ex: It is hard to conceive how the system ran without monitoring for so long.
nat: The founders conceived the idea during a weekend hackathon.

mis.bad: I cannot conceive to live without internet.
mis.good: I cannot conceive of living without internet.
mis.why: Use "conceive of + -ing" or "conceive + noun/how-clause".

def: Giving a lot of information clearly and in a few words.
ex: Keep your status update concise so everyone can read it in thirty seconds.
nat: Her summary was remarkably concise and accurate.

mis.bad: Please write a concise resume with 10 pages.
mis.good: Please write a concise summary in three lines.
mis.why: "Concise" specifically means brief and to the point.

def: To severely restrict the scope, extent, or activity of something.
ex: Tight memory limits constrain how much data we can cache locally.
nat: Budget cuts constrained our ability to hire new staff.

mis.bad: The rules constrained us to do nothing.
mis.good: The rules constrained our options.
mis.why: More naturally used with nouns ("constrain our options") or passive ("feel constrained").

def: To seek information or advice from someone with expertise.
ex: You should consult the security team before opening that port.
nat: I always consult the documentation before changing a config file.

mis.bad: Let me consult with the manual.
mis.good: Let me consult the manual.
mis.why: Use "consult + thing" (manual, doctor) without "with"; "consult with" is for peers/colleagues.

def: To think deeply and at length about something, or to consider doing it.
ex: She is contemplating moving abroad for a senior engineering role.
nat: We briefly contemplated rewriting the entire module from scratch.

mis.bad: I am contemplating to change my job.
mis.good: I am contemplating changing my job.
mis.why: "Contemplate" is followed by -ing, never "to + infinitive".

def: To have a mutual relationship or connection in which one thing affects or depends on another.
ex: High page load times strongly correlate with lower user retention.
nat: Test scores do not always correlate with real-world performance.

mis.bad: Sleep correlates to productivity.
mis.good: Sleep correlates with productivity.
mis.why: Always pair "correlate" with "with", not "to".

def: A detailed analysis and assessment of something, especially a theory or work.
ex: The architect gave a constructive critique of our database schema.
nat: Her critique focused on scalability rather than code style.

mis.bad: He made a critique to my presentation.
mis.good: He gave a critique of my presentation.
mis.why: Use "give/offer a critique of something", not "make a critique to".

def: To reduce in extent or quantity; to impose a restriction on.
ex: Rising cloud costs forced us to curtail non-essential background jobs.
nat: Travel restrictions curtailed international conferences for two years.

mis.bad: We must curtail down the expenses.
mis.good: We must curtail the expenses.
mis.why: Do not add "down" after "curtail"; it already means reduce.

def: To arrive at a fact or conclusion by reasoning from available evidence.
ex: From the stack trace, we can deduce that the token expired mid-request.
nat: Police deduced the suspect had entered through a side window.

mis.bad: I deduced that he left by his empty desk.
mis.good: I deduced from his empty desk that he had left.
mis.why: Use "deduce [something] from [evidence]".

def: To put off an action or event to a later time; to postpone.
ex: Let us defer that architectural decision until we have real traffic data.
nat: The committee decided to defer the vote until next month.

mis.bad: We deferred the meeting for next week.
mis.good: We deferred the meeting until next week.
mis.why: Use "until" or "to" for the new date, not "for".

def: To represent or show something in a picture, story, or diagram.
ex: The diagram depicts how requests flow from the gateway to each microservice.
nat: The documentary depicts daily life in a remote Arctic town.

mis.bad: The chart depicts about monthly sales.
mis.good: The chart depicts monthly sales.
mis.why: "Depict" is transitive and takes no "about".

def: To discourage someone from doing something by instilling doubt or fear of consequences.
ex: Multi-factor authentication helps deter automated credential attacks.
nat: High fees deterred many small businesses from joining the platform.

mis.bad: The price deterred me to buy it.
mis.good: The price deterred me from buying it.
mis.why: Always use "deter someone from + -ing".

def: To depart from an established course, norm, or plan.
ex: Do not deviate from the deployment checklist during a release.
nat: Temperatures rarely deviate much from the seasonal average.

mis.bad: He deviated of the original plan.
mis.good: He deviated from the original plan.
mis.why: Use "deviate from", not "of".

def: To plan or invent a complex procedure, system, or mechanism by careful thought.
ex: We need to devise a faster recovery plan for database outages.
nat: Engineers devised an algorithm that predicts battery wear.

mis.bad: They devised to build a new tool.
mis.good: They devised a way to build a new tool.
mis.why: "Devise" takes a noun object (a plan, a way), not a "to" infinitive.

def: To make or become less in size, importance, or strength.
ex: Repeated delays can diminish user trust in the product.
nat: His enthusiasm did not diminish despite the setbacks.

mis.bad: The risk diminished down over time.
mis.good: The risk diminished over time.
mis.why: Do not add "down" after "diminish".

def: To spread information, knowledge, or ideas widely.
ex: The security team will disseminate the updated guidelines to all offices.
nat: Journals exist to disseminate peer-reviewed research.

mis.bad: They disseminated the news for everyone.
mis.good: They disseminated the news to everyone.
mis.why: Use "disseminate [something] to [people]".

def: To pull or twist out of shape, or give a misleading account of facts.
ex: Outliers can easily distort the average response time in your metrics.
nat: The article distorted his remarks by quoting them out of context.

mis.bad: The microphone distorted with my voice.
mis.good: The microphone distorted my voice.
mis.why: "Distort" is transitive; omit "with".

def: To cause someone or something to change course or turn from one use to another.
ex: During maintenance, we divert all incoming traffic to the backup region.
nat: The flight was diverted to Manchester due to heavy fog.

mis.bad: They diverted the budget for marketing.
mis.good: They diverted the budget to marketing.
mis.why: Use "divert [something] from X to Y".

def: A specified sphere of activity, knowledge, or internet address space.
ex: Natural language processing is a fast-moving domain within AI.
nat: This question falls outside my domain of expertise.

mis.bad: That topic is not of my domain.
mis.good: That topic is outside my domain.
mis.why: Say "outside my domain" or "within my domain".

def: Able to withstand wear, pressure, or damage over a long time.
ex: Invest in durable hardware if the team travels every week.
nat: Stainless steel is far more durable than cheap plastic.

mis.bad: This battery is very durable for years.
mis.good: This battery is durable and lasts for years.
mis.why: "Durable" describes inherent quality, not duration with "for".

def: To develop or present a theory, policy, or system in further detail.
ex: Could you elaborate on why the migration took twice as long?
nat: She promised to elaborate on the proposal during tomorrow's call.

mis.bad: Could you elaborate more about your point?
mis.good: Could you elaborate on your point?
mis.why: Always use "elaborate on [something]", not "about".

def: To evoke or draw out a reaction, answer, or fact from someone.
ex: Open-ended questions help elicit honest feedback from users.
nat: The announcement elicited strong reactions from the community.

mis.bad: The survey elicited for honest opinions.
mis.good: The survey elicited honest opinions.
mis.why: "Elicit" is transitive (no "for"); do not confuse with "illicit" (illegal).

def: To fix an object or piece of code firmly and deeply into a surrounding mass or system.
ex: You can embed the analytics widget directly inside the dashboard.
nat: Security checks should be embedded into every stage of delivery.

mis.bad: We embedded the script inside of the page.
mis.good: We embedded the script in the page.
mis.why: Use "embed [something] in/into [something]".

def: To move out of or away from something and become visible or known.
ex: New AI safety frameworks continue to emerge every few months.
nat: A clear pattern began to emerge once we plotted the errors.

mis.bad: A new problem was emerged yesterday.
mis.good: A new problem emerged yesterday.
mis.why: "Emerge" is intransitive; never use it in the passive ("was emerged").

def: Based on, concerned with, or verifiable by observation or experience rather than theory alone.
ex: We need empirical evidence before rolling out this change to all users.
nat: The study provides strong empirical support for spaced repetition.

mis.bad: That is just an empirical guess without proof.
mis.good: That is a theoretical guess without empirical proof.
mis.why: "Empirical" means backed by real observation/data, the opposite of a guess.

def: To declare one's public approval or support of someone or something.
ex: The security board refused to endorse the unencrypted protocol.
nat: Several industry leaders endorsed the open-source standard.

mis.bad: The team endorsed with the new policy.
mis.good: The team endorsed the new policy.
mis.why: "Endorse" takes a direct object with no "with".

def: To compel observance of or compliance with a law, rule, or obligation.
ex: The gateway will automatically enforce rate limits on public endpoints.
nat: Rules are useless if nobody enforces them consistently.

mis.bad: We need to reinforce the password rules.
mis.good: We need to enforce the password rules.
mis.why: "Reinforce" means strengthen; "enforce" means make sure a rule is obeyed.

def: To involve something as a necessary or inevitable part or consequence.
ex: Migrating to a new cloud provider will entail weeks of regression testing.
nat: What does the senior architect role actually entail?

mis.bad: This job entails to travel frequently.
mis.good: This job entails traveling frequently.
mis.why: "Entail" takes a noun or -ing form, not "to + infinitive".

def: Not even or regular in pattern or movement; unpredictable.
ex: Users complained about erratic network speeds throughout the afternoon.
nat: His sleep schedule became erratic during the product launch.

mis.bad: The server had an errant response time.
mis.good: The server had erratic response times.
mis.why: "Errant" means straying/misbehaving; "erratic" means irregular/unpredictable.

def: To escape or avoid something, especially by cleverness or trickery.
ex: Attackers tried to evade detection by splitting the payload across requests.
nat: He skillfully evaded every direct question during the interview.

mis.bad: The malware evaded from the antivirus.
mis.good: The malware evaded the antivirus.
mis.why: "Evade" is transitive; do not use "from".

def: To make a problem, bad situation, or negative feeling worse.
ex: Running heavy batch jobs at noon will only exacerbate the database bottleneck.
nat: Lack of sleep often exacerbates stress at work.

mis.bad: The delay exacerbated more the conflict.
mis.good: The delay exacerbated the conflict even further.
mis.why: "Exacerbate" already means make worse; never pair it with "more".

def: Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion or doubt.
ex: The API requires explicit user consent before accessing location data.
nat: She gave explicit instructions on how to rotate the keys.

mis.bad: He was explicit with his expectations.
mis.good: He was explicit about his expectations.
mis.why: Use "explicit about [something]".

def: To omit or decline to take something pleasant or valuable; to go without.
ex: The startup decided to forgo short-term profits to invest in reliability.
nat: I had to forgo lunch to finish the incident report on time.

mis.bad: I decided to forgo from the bonus.
mis.good: I decided to forgo the bonus.
mis.why: "Forgo" is transitive and takes no "from".

def: Conflict or resistance that slows down a process or interaction.
ex: Removing extra form fields reduced signup friction by thirty percent.
nat: Poor handoffs create unnecessary friction between product and QA.

mis.bad: There are many frictions in the checkout.
mis.good: There is a lot of friction in the checkout.
mis.why: "Friction" is uncountable in English.

def: To estimate or determine the magnitude, amount, or volume of something.
ex: We ran a quick survey to gauge customer satisfaction after the redesign.
nat: It is hard to gauge how long a legacy refactor will take.

mis.bad: Let us gauge about user feedback.
mis.good: Let us gauge user feedback.
mis.why: "Gauge" is transitive (no "about"); note the spelling "-au-".

def: Characterized by a high level of detail or small, distinct components.
ex: Role-based access gives us granular control over who can export reports.
nat: The new dashboard offers a much more granular view of daily traffic.

mis.bad: We need a granularly control of permissions.
mis.good: We need granular control over permissions.
mis.why: Use the adjective "granular" before a noun, not the adverb.

def: To control and make use of a resource or force to produce power or results.
ex: Modern teams harness automation to eliminate repetitive manual checks.
nat: Coastal regions can harness wind energy all year round.

mis.bad: We should harness with AI tools.
mis.good: We should harness AI tools.
mis.why: "Harness" takes a direct object without "with".

def: To create difficulties for someone or something, resulting in delay or obstruction.
ex: Outdated tooling can severely hinder a team's ability to ship safely.
nat: Heavy snow hindered rescue efforts overnight.

mis.bad: Slow tests hinder us to deploy fast.
mis.good: Slow tests hinder us from deploying fast.
mis.why: Use "hinder [someone/something] from + -ing", or "hinder [noun]".

def: To involve oneself deeply in a particular activity or interest.
ex: The fastest way to progress is to immerse yourself in English podcasts every day.
nat: She immersed herself in the new codebase over the weekend.

mis.bad: I immersed in the documentation.
mis.good: I immersed myself in the documentation.
mis.why: Use the reflexive pronoun ("immerse yourself/myself in") when talking about a person.

def: To weaken or damage something, especially a human faculty or system function.
ex: Poor indexing can severely impair query performance as the table grows.
nat: Lack of sleep impairs both judgment and reaction time.

mis.bad: The bug impaired to load the page.
mis.good: The bug impaired page loading.
mis.why: "Impair" takes a noun object, not a "to" infinitive.

def: To delay or prevent someone or something by obstructing them.
ex: Unclear requirements often impede progress during the first sprint.
nat: Fallen trees impeded traffic along the main highway.

mis.bad: That rule impedes us to deploy.
mis.good: That rule impedes our deployment.
mis.why: Unlike "prevent ... from", "impede" normally takes a direct noun object.

def: Suggested though not directly expressed.
ex: There was an implicit assumption that the service would stay online 24/7.
nat: Her silence felt like an implicit endorsement of the plan.

mis.bad: He made an implicit warning for us.
mis.good: He gave us an implicit warning.
mis.why: Use "give/issue a warning", not "make a warning".

def: To force an unwelcome decision, rule, or tax to be accepted or put in place.
ex: The firewall rules impose strict limits on outbound connections.
nat: The city imposed a fine on companies that missed the deadline.

mis.bad: They imposed us a new deadline.
mis.good: They imposed a new deadline on us.
mis.why: Use "impose [something] on [someone]".

pt: incorrer em / gerar custo ou risco
def: To become subject to something unwelcome or unpleasant as a result of one's own behavior or actions.
ex: Leaving unused GPU instances running overnight will incur high cloud charges.
nat: Late payments may incur an additional administrative fee.

mis.bad: We incurred in extra expenses.
mis.good: We incurred extra expenses.
mis.why: "Incur" is transitive; do not use "in" after it.

def: To succeed in persuading or leading someone to do something, or to bring about a state.
ex: Sudden traffic spikes can induce cascading failures across microservices.
nat: Nothing could induce him to change his mind.

mis.bad: The error induced the system crashing.
mis.good: The error induced the system to crash.
mis.why: Use "induce [someone/something] to + base verb" or "induce [noun]".

def: To hinder, restrain, or prevent an action or process.
ex: Fear of making mistakes can inhibit learners from speaking freely.
nat: Certain chemicals inhibit bacterial growth.

mis.bad: Shyness inhibits me to speak.
mis.good: Shyness inhibits me from speaking.
mis.why: Always use "inhibit [someone] from + -ing".

def: To cause a process or action to begin.
ex: Click the button to initiate an automated backup of the database.
nat: The company initiated a formal investigation into the breach.

mis.bad: We initiated to migrate the data.
mis.good: We initiated the data migration.
mis.why: "Initiate" takes a noun object, not a "to" infinitive.

def: To come between so as to prevent or alter a result or course of events.
ex: An engineer had to intervene manually when the rollback stalled.
nat: The central bank intervened to stabilize the currency.

mis.bad: The manager intervened the conflict.
mis.good: The manager intervened in the conflict.
mis.why: "Intervene" is intransitive; use "intervene in [a situation]".

def: Belonging naturally; essential to the nature of something.
ex: Continuous learning is an intrinsic part of working in cybersecurity.
nat: Gold has an intrinsic value beyond its use in jewelry.

mis.bad: Curiosity is intrinsic for scientists.
mis.good: Curiosity is intrinsic to scientists.
mis.why: Use "intrinsic to", not "for".

def: To cite or appeal to someone or something as an authority, or to call a function in code.
ex: The webhook will invoke the billing service as soon as payment clears.
nat: She invoked the emergency clause to pause the contract.

mis.bad: The script invoked to the endpoint.
mis.good: The script invoked the endpoint.
mis.why: "Invoke" is transitive and takes no "to".

def: To nullify or make ineffective.
ex: A single unencrypted backup can negate all your other security controls.
nat: Rising inflation negated the effect of the salary increase.

mis.bad: This flaw negates against our progress.
mis.good: This flaw negates our progress.
mis.why: "Negate" takes a direct object without "against".

def: To counteract or balance out one effect with an opposing one.
ex: Caching static assets helped offset the higher latency of the new API.
nat: They planted trees to offset the carbon emissions of the flight.

mis.bad: The bonus offsetted the extra hours.
mis.good: The bonus offset the extra hours.
mis.why: The past tense and past participle of "offset" is "offset", never "offsetted".

def: To leave out or exclude someone or something, either intentionally or forgetfully.
ex: Never omit error handling in production scripts, even for small tasks.
nat: She accidentally omitted her phone number from the form.

mis.bad: He omitted to say his name.
mis.good: He omitted his name.
mis.why: "Omit" is clearest with a noun object or "omit + -ing".

def: To extend over so as to cover partly, or have areas in common.
ex: Our work schedules overlap by three hours each morning despite the time zone difference.
nat: The two roles overlap in several key responsibilities.

mis.bad: My meeting overlaps to yours.
mis.good: My meeting overlaps with yours.
mis.why: Use "overlap with", not "to".

def: A seemingly absurd or self-contradictory statement or situation that may nonetheless be true.
ex: It is a paradox that having more productivity tools often leaves us with less time.
nat: The paradox of choice is that too many options can paralyze buyers.

mis.bad: That is a big paradox between them.
mis.good: That is a paradox in their argument.
mis.why: A paradox is an internal contradiction, not a disagreement between two people.

def: To become aware or conscious of something, or interpret it in a particular way.
ex: Users often perceive a site as slow if there is no loading indicator.
nat: How customers perceive your brand matters as much as the product itself.

mis.bad: I perceived that he was tired when I looked his face.
mis.good: I noticed that he was tired when I saw his face.
mis.why: "Perceive" is formal and fits impressions/attitudes ("perceive X as Y"); use "notice" for quick visual observation.

def: To continue firmly in an opinion or course of action despite difficulty, or continue to exist.
ex: If the connection error persists after restarting, check the firewall logs.
nat: She persisted in asking tough questions until the root cause was clear.

mis.bad: He persisted to try.
mis.good: He persisted in trying.
mis.why: Use "persist in + -ing", not "to + infinitive".

def: Relevant or applicable to a particular matter.
ex: Please keep your questions pertinent to the security audit on the agenda.
nat: She raised several pertinent points during the architecture review.

mis.bad: That comment is pertinent for our discussion.
mis.good: That comment is pertinent to our discussion.
mis.why: Use "pertinent to", not "for".

def: To come before something in time, order, or position.
ex: A brief warm-up block will precede the main grammar exercises.
nat: Heavy dark clouds usually precede a summer storm.

mis.bad: Monday precedes to Tuesday.
mis.good: Monday precedes Tuesday.
mis.why: "Precede" is transitive and never takes "to".

def: To prevent from happening; to make impossible.
ex: A tight budget does not preclude building a clean, reliable product.
nat: His injury precluded him from competing in the final match.

mis.bad: Lack of time precludes us to test everything.
mis.good: Lack of time precludes us from testing everything.
mis.why: Use "preclude [someone] from + -ing".

def: Present as the strongest or main element.
ex: English remains the predominant language of international technical documentation.
nat: Cost was the predominant factor in choosing the cloud provider.

mis.bad: This is the most predominant reason.
mis.good: This is the predominant reason.
mis.why: "Predominant" already means main/chief; avoid "most predominant".

def: A previous statement or proposition from which another is inferred or follows as a conclusion.
ex: The whole design rests on the premise that users want instant feedback.
nat: Your conclusion makes sense, but I disagree with your basic premise.

mis.bad: We started from a wrong premise in the office.
mis.good: We started from a false premise.
mis.why: In logic/arguments, pair "premise" with "false", "flawed", or "basic", not "wrong".

def: To prove more powerful than opposing forces; to be widespread or current.
ex: Common sense usually prevails when the team reviews metrics instead of opinions.
nat: Optimism prevailed despite the tight launch deadline.

mis.bad: The new standard prevailed the old one.
mis.good: The new standard prevailed over the old one.
mis.why: Use "prevail over" or "prevail against".

def: To formally forbid something by law, rule, or other authority.
ex: Company policy strictly prohibits storing plaintext credentials in repositories.
nat: Smoking is prohibited anywhere inside the building.

mis.bad: The rule prohibits us to share passwords.
mis.good: The rule prohibits us from sharing passwords.
mis.why: Use "prohibit [someone] from + -ing".

def: To increase rapidly in numbers; to multiply.
ex: AI coding assistants have proliferated across software teams over the last two years.
nat: Small coffee shops began to proliferate throughout the neighborhood.

mis.bad: New apps are proliferating themselves fast.
mis.good: New apps are proliferating fast.
mis.why: "Proliferate" is intransitive; do not add "themselves".

def: To spread and promote an idea, signal, or change widely.
ex: It can take up to an hour for DNS changes to propagate worldwide.
nat: Sound waves propagate much faster through water than through air.

mis.bad: The update propagated to all servers by itself.
mis.good: The update propagated across all servers.
mis.why: Use "propagate through/across" for networks or systems.

def: To stimulate or give rise to a reaction or emotion, typically a strong or unwelcome one.
ex: Changing the pricing model overnight will inevitably provoke customer backlash.
nat: The memo provoked a lively debate among senior engineers.

mis.bad: His comment provoked me to get angry.
mis.good: His comment made me angry / provoked an angry reaction.
mis.why: Say "provoke a reaction/debate" or "provoke someone into + -ing".

def: Acting with or showing care and thought for the future.
ex: It is prudent to keep an offline backup before running a major schema migration.
nat: She made a prudent decision to diversify her savings.

mis.bad: He is very prudent with his words when driving.
mis.good: He is very careful when driving / prudent with his finances.
mis.why: "Prudent" is used for foresight in decisions, risks, and money, not physical driving.

def: To express or measure the quantity of something.
ex: Always try to quantify the impact of your project on your resume.
nat: It is difficult to quantify how much time poor documentation wastes.

mis.bad: We need to quantify how many hours it took in numbers.
mis.good: We need to quantify how many hours it took.
mis.why: "Quantify" already means put into numbers; omit "in numbers".

def: To improve an idea, method, or substance by making small changes.
ex: We spent two weeks refining the onboarding flow based on user recordings.
nat: The model is refined continuously as new training data arrives.

mis.bad: Let us refine more this paragraph.
mis.good: Let us refine this paragraph further.
mis.why: Use "further" instead of "more" with "refine".

def: To prove a statement or theory to be wrong or false; to disprove.
ex: The benchmark results clearly refute the claim that the new parser is slower.
nat: She presented fresh data to refute her colleague's hypothesis.

mis.bad: He refuted to accept the offer.
mis.good: He refused to accept the offer.
mis.why: "Refuse" means say no to an offer/request; "refute" means prove a claim false.

def: To say something again or a number of times, typically for emphasis or clarity.
ex: Let me reiterate that no customer data was exposed during the incident.
nat: The CEO reiterated the company's commitment to remote work.

mis.bad: Let me reiterate again what I said.
mis.good: Let me reiterate what I said.
mis.why: "Reiterate" already means say again; never say "reiterate again".

def: A means of counteracting or eliminating something undesirable, such as an error or problem.
ex: Adding an index on the user ID column was a quick remedy for the slow query.
nat: There is no instant remedy for decades of underinvestment.

mis.bad: We need a remedy against this bug.
mis.good: We need a remedy for this bug.
mis.why: Use "remedy for [a problem]", not "against".

pt: tornar / deixar em certo estado / renderizar
def: To cause to be or become; or to display graphics/HTML on a screen.
ex: A single missing bracket can render the entire configuration file invalid.
nat: The storm rendered the mountain road completely impassable.

mis.bad: The error rendered the app to crash.
mis.good: The error rendered the app unusable.
mis.why: "Render" takes [object] + [adjective] ("rendered it useless"), not "to + verb".

def: To continue to have something; to keep possession of.
ex: Spaced repetition helps you retain new vocabulary months after first seeing it.
nat: The company struggled to retain senior engineers.

mis.bad: We need to retain back our best clients.
mis.good: We need to retain our best clients.
mis.why: "Retain" already means keep; omit "back".

def: To get or bring something back from somewhere, especially stored data.
ex: The service can retrieve user preferences from cache in under five milliseconds.
nat: I had to go back to the office to retrieve my badge.

mis.bad: We retrieved the file of the backup.
mis.good: We retrieved the file from the backup.
mis.why: Always use "retrieve [something] from [source]".

def: To examine or inspect closely and thoroughly.
ex: Security reviewers scrutinize every pull request that touches authentication.
nat: Regulators are scrutinizing how large platforms handle user data.

mis.bad: They scrutinized into the logs.
mis.good: They scrutinized the logs.
mis.why: "Scrutinize" is transitive; omit "into".

def: Not easily convinced; having doubts or reservations.
ex: Engineers were skeptical that a rewrite could finish in three months.
nat: I am a bit skeptical about claims that sound too good to be true.

mis.bad: I am skeptical with that vendor.
mis.good: I am skeptical about that vendor.
mis.why: Use "skeptical about" or "skeptical of", not "with".

def: Not involving anyone or anything else; only.
ex: Do not rely solely on multiple-choice questions to measure speaking ability.
nat: The decision was based solely on cost rather than quality.

mis.bad: He is solely the person who knows.
mis.good: He is the only person who knows.
mis.why: Use "solely" before verbs/prepositional phrases ("solely responsible", "rely solely on"); use "the only" before nouns.

def: Occurring at irregular intervals or only in a few places; scattered or isolated.
ex: Sporadic timeouts are the hardest bugs to reproduce locally.
nat: There were only sporadic showers throughout the afternoon.

mis.bad: We had sporadic meetings every Monday.
mis.good: We had regular meetings every Monday, with sporadic extra calls.
mis.why: "Sporadic" means irregular/unscheduled, never "every Monday".

def: To cease developing; to become inactive or dull.
ex: Without regular speaking practice, your fluency can easily stagnate at B1.
nat: Wage growth has stagnated despite rising living costs.

mis.bad: Sales were stagnated in June.
mis.good: Sales stagnated in June.
mis.why: "Stagnate" is intransitive; avoid "were stagnated" unless using the adjective "stagnant".

def: Coming after something in time; following.
ex: Subsequent releases fixed the memory leak without any downtime.
nat: The error appeared during login and in all subsequent requests.

mis.bad: The subsequent day after the launch was calm.
mis.good: The day after the launch was calm / Subsequent days were calm.
mis.why: "Subsequent" is formal and usually modifies plural nouns or events ("subsequent releases"), not "the subsequent day after".

def: To provide evidence to support or prove the truth of a claim.
ex: Please include benchmark numbers to substantiate your performance claim.
nat: The report failed to substantiate any of the serious allegations.

mis.bad: Can you substantiate about your theory?
mis.good: Can you substantiate your theory?
mis.why: "Substantiate" is transitive and takes no "about".

def: To take the place of a person or thing previously in authority or use.
ex: This v2 protocol will supersede the legacy XML format next year.
nat: Smartphones have largely superseded standalone digital cameras.

mis.bad: The new rule superceded the old one.
mis.good: The new rule superseded the old one.
mis.why: Spell it "-sede" (with an "s"), not "-cede".

def: To add an extra element or amount to something to complete or enhance it.
ex: Short daily sessions should supplement real listening and conversation, not replace them.
nat: She supplemented her income by doing freelance design work.

mis.bad: This course supplements to my studies.
mis.good: This course supplements my studies.
mis.why: As a verb, "supplement" is transitive (no "to").

def: To forcibly put an end to, or prevent the dissemination or display of something.
ex: Never suppress exceptions silently; always log them with context.
nat: The medication helps suppress the allergic reaction.

mis.bad: He suppressed to show his anger.
mis.good: He suppressed his anger.
mis.why: "Suppress" takes a noun object, not a "to" infinitive.

def: To exceed; to be greater than.
ex: Quarterly revenue surpassed our most optimistic forecast by twelve percent.
nat: Her final presentation surpassed everyone's expectations.

mis.bad: Our results surpassed than last year.
mis.good: Our results surpassed last year's.
mis.why: "Surpass" is transitive; never use "than" after it.

def: To strengthen or support physically or mentally, or keep something going over time.
ex: Can the current infrastructure sustain ten times more concurrent users?
nat: It is hard to sustain focus for three hours without a short break.

mis.bad: We cannot sustain to work 12 hours a day.
mis.good: We cannot sustain working 12 hours a day.
mis.why: Use "sustain + noun/-ing", not "to + infinitive".

def: Easy to perceive or detect; open and honest without hidden agendas.
ex: Be transparent with stakeholders when a milestone is at risk of slipping.
nat: The pricing page should be completely transparent about hidden fees.

mis.bad: They were transparent for the team.
mis.good: They were transparent with the team.
mis.why: Use "transparent with [people] about [something]".

def: To underline or emphasize the importance of something.
ex: Recent breaches underscore the need for zero-trust access controls.
nat: The survey results underscore how much users value speed.

mis.bad: I want to underscore about this risk.
mis.good: I want to underscore this risk.
mis.why: "Underscore" is transitive and takes no "about".

def: To make or become united, uniform, or whole.
ex: Our goal is to unify login across all five internal tools with single sign-on.
nat: A shared design system helped unify the look of mobile and web apps.

mis.bad: We need to unify into one single API.
mis.good: We need to unify everything into a single API.
mis.why: "Unify" is usually transitive ("unify X and Y into Z").

def: To confirm or support something that has been questioned, such as a law or standard.
ex: Every code reviewer helps uphold our engineering quality standards.
nat: The appeals court upheld the earlier ruling.

mis.bad: We must uphold with our principles.
mis.good: We must uphold our principles.
mis.why: "Uphold" takes a direct object without "with".

def: To make practical and effective use of.
ex: The scheduler can utilize idle CPU cores during off-peak hours.
nat: Make sure you utilize all the available practice modes in the app.

mis.bad: I utilize a pen to sign.
mis.good: I use a pen to sign.
mis.why: In everyday speech, "use" is more natural; save "utilize" for making effective use of resources/capacity.

def: Capable of working successfully; feasible.
ex: Running a local server is a viable option when cloud hosting is not allowed.
nat: Solar power has become an economically viable alternative.

mis.bad: This plan is viable to work.
mis.good: This plan is viable.
mis.why: Do not add "to work" after "viable"; "viable" already means capable of working.

def: To justify or necessitate a certain course of action.
ex: A minor typo does not warrant rolling back the entire release.
nat: The spike in failed logins warrants an immediate security review.

mis.bad: This issue warrants for an urgent fix.
mis.good: This issue warrants an urgent fix.
mis.why: "Warrant" is transitive and takes no "for".

def: To remain undamaged or unaffected by; to resist successfully.
ex: The payment gateway is built to withstand sudden Black Friday traffic spikes.
nat: Modern bridges are engineered to withstand strong earthquakes.

mis.bad: The server withstood against the attack.
mis.good: The server withstood the attack.
mis.why: "Withstand" is transitive; do not use "against".

def: To produce or provide a natural, agricultural, or industrial product or result; or to give way.
ex: Adding targeted examples will yield much better retention than memorizing lists.
nat: The experiment yielded surprising insights into user behavior.

mis.bad: This strategy yielded us many benefits.
mis.good: This strategy yielded great benefits for us.
mis.why: Usually "yield [results/benefits]" without an indirect object before it.

def: A secret word or code you type to enter a system or account.
ex: You should change your password every few months to keep your account safe.
nat: I forgot my password, so I asked the system to send me a reset link.

mis.bad: Please digit your password.
mis.good: Please type your password.
mis.why: "Digitar" is "type" in English; "digit" only means a number character like 5.

def: To copy a file from the internet to your own device.
ex: I downloaded the report to my laptop so I could read it on the train.
nat: You can download the app for free from the official website.

mis.bad: I did the download of the file yesterday.
mis.good: I downloaded the file yesterday.
mis.why: Use download as a verb (downloaded) instead of "do the download of".

def: To send a file from your device to the internet or another system.
ex: She uploaded the photos to the shared folder before the meeting started.
nat: It took ages to upload the video because the connection was so slow.

mis.bad: I uploaded the file in the cloud.
mis.good: I uploaded the file to the cloud.
mis.why: Use "to" with upload, not "in", when you send a file to a place.

def: To put a program on a computer so that it is ready to use.
ex: I installed the new software yesterday, but it still doesn't open properly.
nat: You need to install the latest version before you can join the call.

mis.bad: I need to instal the program.
mis.good: I need to install the program.
mis.why: In English the verb is spelled with two l's: install.

def: Programs and instructions that make a computer do tasks.
ex: Our company buys software from several suppliers to manage its customer data.
nat: This software is easy to learn, even for people with no experience.

mis.bad: I bought two softwares for the office.
mis.good: I bought two pieces of software for the office.
mis.why: Software is uncountable, so it has no plural; say "a piece of software".

def: A group of computers or devices that are connected to share information.
ex: The whole office lost internet access because of a problem with the network.
nat: Please connect to the guest network if you are visiting our office.

mis.bad: I connected in the network.
mis.good: I connected to the network.
mis.why: Connect takes "to".

def: A powerful computer that stores data and provides services to other computers.
ex: The website went down for an hour because the server ran out of memory.
nat: We moved all our files to a new server last weekend.

mis.bad: The servant is not responding.
mis.good: The server is not responding.
mis.why: "Servant" means a person who serves; for a computer, use server.

def: A set of connected pages on the internet with one address.
ex: Our website gets about ten thousand visitors every day, mostly from mobile phones.
nat: I couldn't find the price on their website, so I called the shop.

mis.bad: I saw it in the site of the company.
mis.good: I saw it on the company's website.
mis.why: Use "on" for websites, not "in": on the website.

def: A program you use to look at pages on the internet.
ex: If the page looks strange, try opening it in a different browser.
nat: I cleared the cache in my browser, and then the site loaded normally.

mis.bad: I opened the navigator and searched for it.
mis.good: I opened the browser and searched for it.
mis.why: "Navegador" is "browser" in English; "navigator" is not used for this.

def: A computer program designed to do a particular job, often called an app.
ex: This application helps small teams plan their projects and share files easily.
nat: She developed a mobile application that tracks how much water you drink.

mis.bad: She works with application development of mobile.
mis.good: She works in mobile application development.
mis.why: Put the modifier first: "mobile application development".

def: A useful part or function of a product or program.
ex: The new camera has a feature that automatically blurs the background of photos.
nat: One feature I really like is the dark mode at night.

mis.bad: This phone has many functionalities.
mis.good: This phone has many features.
mis.why: "Functionalities" is rarely used; say "features" for what a product can do.

def: A mistake in a program that makes it work incorrectly.
ex: The developers are working to fix a bug that deletes saved settings.
nat: We found a serious bug just before the product launch.

mis.bad: The program has a lot of erros.
mis.good: The program has a lot of bugs.
mis.why: In software, a mistake in the code is a bug, not an "error" in everyday speech about problems.

def: Instructions written in a programming language for a computer.
ex: He spent the whole afternoon reading old code to understand how the system works.
nat: Please add comments to your code so other people can understand it.

mis.bad: I am learning to code in Python language.
mis.good: I am learning to code in Python.
mis.why: Say "in Python"; adding the word "language" is unnecessary and sounds strange.

def: Unwanted messages, usually advertising, sent to many people by email.
ex: Most of the emails I get every morning are spam, so I delete them quickly.
nat: My email filter catches almost all the spam before I see it.

mis.bad: I received many spams today.
mis.good: I received a lot of spam today.
mis.why: Spam is uncountable, so it never takes an -s.

def: A personal record with your details that lets you use a service.
ex: You need to create an account before you can buy anything on this site.
nat: She logged in to her account and changed her email address.

mis.bad: I opened an account in the website.
mis.good: I opened an account on the website.
mis.why: Use "on" with websites.

def: Options on a device or program that you can change.
ex: You can turn off notifications in the settings of your phone.
nat: I changed the privacy settings so only my friends can see my photos.

mis.bad: I entered in the configurations of the phone.
mis.good: I opened the settings on the phone.
mis.why: In apps and devices, "configurações" is usually "settings", not "configurations".

def: A device that stores power so a phone or laptop can work without a cable.
ex: My phone battery only lasts half a day now, so I carry a charger.
nat: The battery died during the meeting, and I could not find a socket.

mis.bad: My battery is discharged.
mis.good: My battery is dead.
mis.why: Use "dead" or "flat" for an empty battery; "discharged" is unnatural.

def: Not using cables or wires to connect to a network or device.
ex: We bought wireless headphones so we can walk around while we talk.
nat: The wireless signal is weak in the back room of the house.

mis.bad: I prefer the wireless of the hotel.
mis.good: I prefer the hotel's wireless internet.
mis.why: Wireless is an adjective, so it needs a noun after it, like wireless internet.

def: A link between a device and a network, or between two things.
ex: I lost my connection during the video call, so I had to rejoin.
nat: A stable connection is essential if you want to work from home.

mis.bad: My conection is very bad.
mis.good: My connection is very bad.
mis.why: The spelling is connection with "ct", not "c" like in Portuguese "conexão".

def: A wave that carries information such as a phone call or internet data.
ex: I can't call you from here because there is no signal in the basement.
nat: The phone shows a strong signal, but the internet is still slow.

mis.bad: I have no sign in my phone.
mis.good: I have no signal on my phone.
mis.why: Use signal for phone or wifi reception; "sign" means a symbol or notice.

def: To remove a file, message, or other data from a device.
ex: I accidentally deleted the folder that contained all my photos from the trip.
nat: Please delete the old emails to free up some space.

mis.bad: I deleted my account of the website.
mis.good: I deleted my account on the website.
mis.why: Use "on" with websites and services, not "of".

def: A collection of data stored on a computer under one name.
ex: The file was too large to send by email, so I shared a link.
nat: Save the file on your desktop so you can find it easily.

mis.bad: I saved the archive on my desktop.
mis.good: I saved the file on my desktop.
mis.why: "Archive" is a compressed or stored collection; for a normal computer file, say file.

def: A place on a computer where you keep a group of files together.
ex: I created a separate folder for each client to keep everything organized.
